headline: Rs24bn additional QTA proposed by Discos draws protest from industrial consumers
summary: ISLAMABAD: Industrial consumers on Tuesday protested over a Rs24 billion additional quarterly tariff burden proposed by power companies due to higher capacity charges, variable operation and maintenance (O&M) costs and the impact of system losses, resulting in an estimated tariff impact of around Rs1.30 per unit for three months.A brief intervention from the power division, represented by the chief financial officer (CFO) of the Power Planning and Monitoring Company (PPMC), Naveed Qaisar, was the request at a public hearing that the additional quarterly tariff adjustment (QTA) be applied beginning in the Dec 1, 2026 billing and ending in February 2027.The hearing was presided over by National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) members Amina Ahmed, Maqsood Anwar Khan and Ghulamullah Shaikh, on the request of 11 distribution companies (Discos) to seek approval for charging the additional QTA for the July-September 2026 period. Once approved, the additional QTA would also be applicable to K-Electric under a government decision in place since 2023.Two industrial interveners — Amir Shaikh and Rehan Javed — expressed serious concern over Rs39bn additional capacity payment claims for the quarter against the pre-approved references built into the base tariff, besides the Rs5.6bn impact on variable O&M and Rs7.8bn impact of system losses in monthly fuel charges.Amir Shaikh, from Lahore, said QTAs normally stay negative when fuel cost adjustments (FCAs) are higher than charges to consumers in respective months. This time, however, the industry faced a double shock — positive FCAs throughout the quarter followed by positive QTAs — while the industrial output had gone out on the premise of lower QTAs.He said the major reason appeared to be units sold to selective consumers under theincremental consumption package(ICP) at an unrealistic cost of Rs10 cheaper than normal tariffs, which translated into a higher QTA for all consumers — despite the government’s promise that the impact of the ICP would not be charged to consumers except for ICP beneficiaries.“This is like rubbing salt into our wounds. It is shocking that the QTA has gone up,” he said.Javed, from Karachi, noted the Discos claimed Rs29.25bn of negative impact of the ICP on industrial consumers, saying it was actually an additional burden from all consumers. A series of questions he raised over the data provided by Discos remained unanswered and Nepra did not press for responses either.Javed alleged that the Discos had counted the wrong units and measured against FY2023-24, instead of references set for this year under the notified tariff.“The ‘relief’ shown (the ICP of Rs29.25bn) is not relief received; it hides a cost other consumers pay,” he said, adding that this was not legally covered by any Nepra decision as all consumers were being forced to fill a Rs15 per unit delta.He contended that when every Disco was claiming to have sold more units than the reference, the capacity cost should have reduced. “Why, then, is the capacity claim going up? Is the benefit of the higher sales being lost because of ICP units?”He demanded to defer the incremental units amount in the QTA claim until the full data, as demanded in March and September 2026, had been filed.Cumulatively, all 11 Discos reported that capacity charges during the July-September period had increased by Rs39bn, which also included the impact of system losses on the monthly fuel cost and variable operation and maintenance costs.Seven out of the 11 Discos demanded additional recovery of about Rs37bn on account of capacity charges, variable O&M charges and the impact of T&D losses on monthly FCA. However, a significant portion was offset by negative adjustments of Rs13bn from four other Discos.The highest additional claims came from Islamabad Electric (Rs10.833bn), followed by Rs10.46bn from Faisalabad and Rs7bn from Peshawar Electric. Tribal Electric led with a negative adjustment of Rs5.8bn, followed by Rs4.1bn by Quetta and Rs1.95bn by Hyderabad Electric.In line with policy guidelines issued by the federal government for uniform quarterly adjustments, the QTA determined for Discos for the third quarter of CY2026 will also apply to K-Electric consumers once Nepra issues its judgment.Under the tariff mechanism, changes in fuel cost are passed on to consumers only on a monthly basis through an automatic mechanism, while QTA, on account of variation in power purchase price, capacity charges, variable operation and maintenance costs, use of system charges and including the impact of transmission and distribution losses, is built into the base tariff by the federal government.

headline: Petrol price reduced by Rs3 per litre, diesel remains unchanged
content: The government on Tuesday reduced the price of petrol by Rs3 per litre, marking the eleventhconsecutivedecrease in the rate, but left the price of high-speed diesel unchanged. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs325 per litre, while HSD will remain at Rs358 on Nov 18 (Wednesday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra). The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. Under anarrangementannounced on Nov 2, for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end. On Sept 17, the governmentrolled outthePrime Minister’s Fuel Relief Schemeacross the country to ease the public’s burden amid rising fuel prices due to the Middle East situation. The subsidy scheme applies to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc. The price of HSD has come down from apeak of Rs520.35recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28. The petrol price hadpeaked at Rs458.41on April 3 after beginning itsupward trajectoryfrom Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government hasreintroduceda raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months. SinceJuly 17, the government has been revising fuel prices on a near-daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Prior to this, the government had been announcingweekly revisionsto fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the conflict. The federal government had alsoannouncedtargeted relief measures in April to provide subsidised fuel. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

headline: Jensen Huang says willing to return as Nvidia CEO, 'owns mistakes'
summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Tuesday that he would be willing to return to the post due to an “outpouring of calls” for his reinstatement after hequit last week over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said in a statement he posted on X.It was Huang’s first public statement since he resigned on Thursday following revelations ofextramarital affairs, including with an executive of a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in circumvention of export controls.The turmoil has battered shares in Nvidia, which until recently was the world’s most valuable publicly traded company.Tech tycoonElon Muskand other major AI investors have been calling for Huang’s reinstatement with an open letter that has garnered more than 190,000 signatures.US President Donald Trumpalso signalled on Monday his support for the return of Huang, who has advised him on AI policy and is perhaps the tech industry’s most recognised promoter of artificial intelligence.“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in the statement.He sounded a note of contrition.“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” he said.“I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.”US lawmakers said Tuesday that Huang will appear before three US House committees on Dec 1 for questioning over concerns that China was able to gain access to advanced US chips from Nvidia.

headline: Asian Development Bank approves $500m loan to support Pakistan’s federal pension reforms
summary: The Asian Development Bank (ADB) on Tuesday approved a $500 million results-based loan to help Pakistan reform its federal civil pension system, the Manila-based lending agency said in astatement.The reforms will help contain rising pension-related fiscal pressures, strengthen pension system sustainability, and expand fiscal space for development and social spending, according to the statement.It added that Pakistan’s federal pension spending has grown nearly fivefold since fiscal year 2016 and now exceeds Rs1 trillion a year.“Its longstanding unfunded and noncontributory legacy defined benefit scheme is financed entirely through annual budget allocations, creating growing fiscal pressure as pension obligations increase over time,” the statement highlighted.“Pakistan has taken important steps to strengthen its federal pension system, and this program will help sustain and institutionalise those reforms,” ADB Country Director for Pakistan Emma Fan was quoted as saying.“ADB’s support will help achieve lasting results by strengthening institutions, improving transparency, and supporting a more sustainable pension system,” Fan added.Furthermore, the financing will support the first phase of the government’s Pension Reform Implementation Plan, and the transition to the defined contribution pension scheme, in which federal civil employees appointed from July 2024 are required to participate, said the statement.“ADB’s support will help improve pension management to reduce liabilities, boost financial transparency through digital systems, and enhance pension service delivery and financial literacy among beneficiaries,” it read.In 2024, ADB’s senior economist Aiko Kikkawahad saidthe pension system in Pakistan suffered from low contribution rates, making it unsustainable in the long run.An earlier report by the ADB highlighted Pakistan’s weak pension and insurance systems. Most government positions entail unfunded pensions, where pensions for current employees are financed through tax revenues, according to the report titled ‘Strengthening Pakistan’s Pension and Insurance Systems’.In August, the governmentexecutedagreements with 16 pension fund managers to formally operationalise the Defined Contribution Pension Fund Scheme (DCPFS), launched a year ago for public sector employees as part of major pension reforms aimed at containing the snowballing pension burden on the budget.

headline: Pakistan, Turkmenistan to convene steering committee for TAPI gas pipeline, stress engagement among partner countries
summary: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Tuesday discussed the Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan-India (TAPI) gas pipeline with a delegation led by Turkmenistan’s Foreign Minister Rashid Meredov.The discussion took place at the 6th Session of the Pakistan–Turkmenistan Joint Intergovernmental Commission (JIC), which was held in Islamabad on Tuesday.Meredov had arrived in Pakistan ahead of the 30th meeting of theEconomic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) Council of Ministers, held from November 15-16.The two sides recognised “the importance of political engagement among the participating countries on the technical and commercial aspects of the project”, Dar said in remarks during a joint press stakeout after the talks.Meanwhile, Meredov said that the two sides also agreed to convene a meeting of the steering committee for the project.The 1,800-kilometre pipeline isexpectedto carry 33 billion cubic metres of natural gas every year from Turkmenistan’s Galkynysh — the world’s second-largest gas field — to the Indian city of Fazilka. It will pass through Herat and Kandahar in Afghanistan, and Quetta and Multan in Pakistan.The project has two phases: a free flow phase with an estimated cost of $5-6bn and installation of compressor stations for at least $1.9bn.In June 2023, Pakistan and Turkmenistansigneda joint implementation plan to execute the TAPI gas pipeline project.In September 2024,Afghanistansaid it would begin work on the pipeline. Progress on the TAPI pipeline had been repeatedly delayed because of security issues in conflict-ravaged Afghanistan.Pakistan, Turkmenistan to strengthen cooperationDPM Dar said on Tuesday that the talks between the two countries on trade, investment and regional connectivity were held in “a very cordial and constructive atmosphere, reflecting the longstanding bonds of friendship, mutual respect and goodwill that characterise Pakistan-Turkmenistan’s relationship”.“Pakistan respects Turkmenistan’s policy of permanent neutrality and values our constructive cooperation in regional and international forums.”DPM Dar said that Pakistan and Turkmenistan have signed the protocol of the 6th Session of the Pakistan–Turkmenistan JIC and Programme of Cooperation for the two foreign ministries for the period 2026-2030, as well as a memorandum of understanding on tourism cooperation.“These instruments reflect the shared commitment of Pakistan and Turkmenistan to strengthening institutional cooperation, sustaining regular diplomatic engagement and promoting tourism and people-to-people ties,” the Foreign Office said in a post on X.“Trade, investment and regional connectivity featured prominently in our discussions,” Dar said in his remarks, adding that the two sides had discussed ways to “advance work on a bilateral transit trade framework and explore commercially viable transport links”.They welcomed closer engagement between the business communities and chambers of commerce of the two countries, he said.The foreign ministers also talked about the proposed Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan electricity transmission project and the associated fibre optic communications link, highlighting the need for further assessment of its technical and commercial viability.“Our discussions also covered opportunities to strengthen cooperation in agriculture, industry, tourism, culture, higher education, information technology, health and financial services,” Dar told the media.Meredov told the media that the two sides also considered interaction between the seaports of Chabahar and Gwadar as well as prospects for railway connections through Afghanistan. “Particular attention was paid to the rail viability of routes, tariffs and border procedures,” he said.“I emphasised the central role of dialogue and diplomacy, respect for international law and adherence to the principles of the United Nations Charter in addressing regional and global challenges,” Meredov said.Meredov added that Turkmenistan was planning to arrange a state visit to Islamabad next year.

headline: Finance ministry orders minimum wage compliance
summary: • Ministries asked to submit wage compliance reports, confirm bank transfers• Move follows parliamentary panel’s concerns over wage violations in public sector• Committee suggests placing funds in interest-bearing accounts so returns can be used for workers’ welfareISLAMABAD: Acting on the recommendations of a parliamentary committee, the Ministry of Finance (MoF) has directed all ministries and divisions to ensure payment of minimum wages to employees of their respective attached departments, autonomous corporations and organisations, and submit compliance reports.“All ministries and divisions are requested to please confirm that the minimum wage is being paid by them and their attached departments, as well as autonomous bodies, corporations and organisations working under their administrative control, and that salaries are disbursed through banking channels,” according to an office memorandum issued by the MoF to all ministries.The memorandum also directed ministries to ensure that the government’s decision regarding minimum wages was implemented in letter and spirit.The directive follows repeated reminders from the National Assembly’s Standing Committee on Overseas Pakistanis and Human Resource Development regarding the non-implementation of minimum wage regulations by public sector entities, which, the committee believes, encourages private employers to disregard government-mandated minimum wages.Earlier this month, the committee had asked the ministries of finance and overseas Pakistanis to obtain confirmation from all departments and issue fresh circulars to ensure payment of minimum wages without delay.The committee had also asked the MoF to consider placing workers’ welfare funds in interest-bearing accounts so that the returns could be used for workers’ welfare.On Nov 3, the committee expressed serious concern over the continued failure to implement the revised minimum daily wage rates for employees of the Overseas Pakistanis Foundation (OPF), despite the government’s announcement and parliamentary approval through the federal budget for 2026-27 in June.The committee deplored that while even private sector employers were required to implement the government’s decision, public sector entities had failed to comply even after four months.An official of the Ministry of Overseas Pakistanis had informed the National Assembly committee that the ministry’s board was required to approve the revised minimum daily wage under the prescribed rules and that a board meeting would be convened soon.The committee, however, expressed displeasure over what it described as a disparity in the implementation of government decisions, observing that officers in grades 20 to 22 promptly implement announcements regarding increases in their salaries, perks and privileges but are reluctant to extend the same treatment to low-paid workers.The committee directed that rules be introduced to ensure that revised minimum wages are paid immediately after their announcement, just as government employees receive increased salaries at the beginning of a new fiscal year without having to wait for board approvals.Published in Dawn, November 17th, 2026

headline: Millers seek immediate sugar exports
summary: LAHORE: The Pakis­tan Sugar Mills Asso­cia­tion has urged the government to allow the immediate export of sugar, fully deregulate the sector, and withdraw the notification requiring mills to start crushing promptly.Speaking at a press conference on Monday, PSMA Chairman Asim Ghani Usman asked the government to pay immediate attention to the issues facing the sugar industry and to save the sector from ruin.He said there is a surplus of 1.1 million tonnes of sugar and that the government had promised to allow the export of 600,000 tonnes, but no permission has yet been granted despite reminders.This year, sugarcane has been cultivated over an area approximately 16 per cent larger than before; consequently, sugar production of 8.5 million tonnes is projected for the 2026-27 crushing season and it would be difficult to store any additional stock.Defending the millers’ inability to comply with the Punjab government’s notification to commence the crushing season within 24 hours, Ghani said that starting a mill is a time-consuming process — staff must be called in and boilers must be fired up.On the other hand, far­mers also require time to harvest their sugarcane. In this scenario, how is it possible to make the mills operational immediately?He requested the chief minister to look into these matters and extend the period by 15 days for the commencement of mill operations.Published in Dawn, November 17, 2026

headline: At ECO moot, Dar calls for translating 'collective commitments into concrete action'
summary: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar closed out the 30th meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) Council of Ministers (COM) inIslamabadon Monday with a call for countries to translate their commitments into action.Pakistan, which holds the ECO chairmanship for 2026-27, hosted the meeting under the theme “Reviving Regionalism for a Resilient ECO”.The deputy premier, who chaired the meeting, expressed his “sincere appreciation to all delegations” for their constructive engagement during the meeting.“The deliberations today have reaffirmed our shared commitment to regional economic cooperation and integration,” Dar said.He termed the adoption of the Strategic Goals of Economic Cooperation 2035 an “important milestone in charting the future course of our organisation over the next decade”, saying that it provided a shared framework to advance regional priorities alongside the Islamabad Communiqué.“Our task now is to translate our collective commitments into concrete action,” he added. “This will require clear priorities, realistic timelines, and effective follow-up mechanisms.”He highlighted regional cooperation as a central pillar of Pakistan’s foreign policy and noted that the country had consistently advocated a “stronger, more effective and responsive” ECO that harnessed “geographical proximity, historical bonds and economic complementarities”.Dar underscored Pakistan’s commitment to advancing the ECO agenda as the chair of the organisation and to working with all institutions and member states to strengthen regional connectivity, facilitate intra-regional trade and promote mutually beneficial economic cooperation.He looked forward to welcoming the countries back for the 31st COM meeting in 2027, saying, “Let us build on the momentum generated here so that our next meeting can take stock of tangible progress in advancing our shared priorities.”In addition, he wished Iran success in hosting the upcoming 18th ECO summit on Dec 3-4.The deputy premier thanked all member states, as well as the secretary general and his team, ECO permanent representatives, and senior officials for their support.Later in the day, Dar held amedia briefingon the meeting alongside ECO Secretary General Asad Majeed Khan and Information Minister Attaullah Tarar.Joint communiquéThe COM meeting concluded with the adoption of two documents, including the Strategic Goals of Economic Cooperation 2035 and the Islamabad Communiqué.Pakistan’s mediation efforts hailedIn the Islamabad Communiqué, ECO member states expressed concern over the “challenging geopolitical environment in the region, emphasising the importance of restraint, dialogue and diplomatic engagement, and recognising the important role” of Iran as a founding member of ECO.They expressed support for the mediation efforts undertaken by Pakistan and Qatar, as well as for the recent initiative put forward by Iran “aimed at achieving a dignified resolution of the conflict and ensuring the complete and permanent termination of the current war”.The ECO states commended Pakistan’s “consistent and constructive diplomatic support for ECO Member States and its mediation efforts towards de-escalation during the recent Iran-United States crisis”.They reaffirmed the importance of dialogue, diplomacy, respect for international law and promoting mutual trust. stability and the peaceful resolution of disputes, and calling for continued cooperation within the ECO framework towards lasting peace and stability in the region.The communiqué also highly appreciated Qatar’s “important role as a trusted facilitator of international diplomacy, most notably demonstrated by its mediation efforts at the 81st United Nations General Assembly”.The members commended ECO for “demonstrating that regionalism can remain effective and operational even under conditions of acute geopolitical stress”.The communiqué expressed concern over the humanitarian situation in Gaza after flooding on Nov 6 as winter begins. It urges priority delivery of food, medicine, fuel, heating equipment, tents, shelters, blankets and winter clothing. It also called for an immediate end to “policies of forced displacement and the deliberate deprivation of food” and full implementation of the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire agreement.The organisation rejected “unilateral coercive measures, sanctions and economic pressures and their extraterritorial economic, technological, financial or trade impacts”.It said they are contrary to the UN Charter and international law, adversely affect international peace and security, and undermine the provision of supply chains for food, pharmaceutical, energy and humanitarian assistance.The joint statement also mentioned Afghanistan, a member of the ECO, though seemingly not present at the meeting.ECO acknowledged the need for “continued consultation with member states to address the issues of Afghanistan’s engagement with the organisation in relevant areas, with a view to achieving the country’s full and effective participation once circumstances permit”.They stressed the need for “achieving meaningful progress on concerns of member states for fostering regional cooperation and laying the basis for Afghanistan’s participation in any ECO activities and processes”.Economy and tradeThe meeting expressed support for various documents adopted in the past, including ECO Vision 2025 and the 2021 Ashgabat Consensus for Action. They also welcomed various UN resolutions and initiatives.Members were urged to speed up amendment and implementation of the ECO Trade Agreement (ECOTA), with non-parties to the pact invited to consultations.The communique called for timely implementation of Turkmenistan’s feasibility study on the establishment of joint trade zones within the ECO region. They pointed to the Turkmenistan–Uzbekistan zone as a model and to a proposed trade market at the Altyn Asyr–Incheh Boroun border crossing between Iran and Turkmenistan.It urged joint measures on foreign direct investment, free economic zones, joint manufacturing, e-commerce and digitised customs “single window” systems.The ECO further stressed “expeditious conclusion” of the draft ECO Trade Facilitation Agreement and tasked the Joint Working Group with intensifying its technical negotiations toward the pact’s early finalisation. Pakistan has offered to host the 4th JWG meeting in the third quarter of 2026.The ministers called for more diversified financing, including through the ECO Trade and Development Bank (ECOTDB), whose membership they want expanded.Members were urged to fully implement the ECO Transit Transport Framework Agreement to “unlock the region’s full potential and enhance regional connectivity, trade, and economic development”.The ministers highlighted the ECO Sustainable and Resilient Transport Strategy 2026–2035 as a flagship framework. They also called for transport and transit corridors and better seaport access for landlocked members.The ECO members welcomed Shusha as ECO Tourism Capital 2026 and noted the schedule of future capitals: Lahore (2027), Mary (2028), Karakol (2029) and Aktau (2030).They also welcomed the operationalisation of the ECO Clean Energy Centre in Baku, as well as the “ECO Five-Year Roadmap on minerals cooperation for 2026–2030”, described as the first overarching framework for regional cooperation on minerals, including critical minerals.AI and technologyThe Islamabad Communiqué acknowledged UN actions on AI, including the first Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva on July 6–7.It underlined the need to bridge the AI capacity gap and promote “safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems in the non-military domain for sustainable development”.The statement also recognised the “transformative potential of emerging technologies”, such as AI, blockchain, quantum computing, 5G and robotics. It called for harnessing these technologies for regional prosperity, while noting the need to share experience on mitigating associated risks.Members were encouraged to cooperate on AI through exchanges of best practices, joint capacity-building and training under the ECO Science Foundation, aiming at bridging the “digital and artificial intelligence divide”.The ministers also noted the significance of the ECO Regional ICT Strategy 2026–2030, stressed the security of critical digital infrastructure, and called for cooperation among members in ICT security.They emphasised the “importance of ensuring equal, fair, transparent and non-discriminatory access, particularly for developing countries, to global markets for ICT security products, technologies and services, as a confidence-building measure”.The ECO members encouraged exploring cooperation on the peaceful uses of outer space, including satellite services, and space-based services in support of regional connectivity, disaster risk reduction and environmental monitoring.Araghchi calls for sustainable energy mechanismAt the ECO meeting, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi stressed the need for a reliable and sustainable regional energy mechanism during his address.The Iranian FM spoke about theUS-Israeli war on Iran, which has also resulted in the choking of key fuel supply routes — theStrait of HormuzandBab al-Mandab.“Our region needs not only an independent security framework but also a reliable and sustainable regional energy mechanism to safeguard energy flows, ensure stable supplies, reduce external vulnerabilities and enhance collective resilience against geopolitical shocks and disruptions,” Araghchi said, according to a transcript of his speech provided by the Iranian embassy in Pakistan.Araghchi said ECO was moving “beyond its traditional role towards becoming an effective platform for collective action, strengthened cooperation and joint efforts”. He said the shift would enable member states “to address emerging challenges and contribute to an inclusive and equitable global economic order”.He stressed the need for a “modern, new-generation, more inclusive, effective and operational trade agreement” that would benefit the region.Referring to the US war on Iran, Araghchi said, “Iran has remained committed to diplomatic engagement and peaceful solutions.”He added, however, that the US had opted for a different course of action, which was “marked by aggression, threats, targeted assassinations, economic coercion, and blockades, in flagrant violation of international law and the UN Charter”.He underscored that Iran had “no inherent dispute” with countries in the region, adding that “the territories, airspace and facilities of the regional countries must not be used as platforms for launching attacks against each other”.“Iran’s legitimate defensive measures are directed exclusively at the targets and military bases of the aggressors and should in no way be construed as actions against the peoples or governments of the neighbouring countries,” Araghchi said.He also called attention toPalestine, describing the genocide in Gaza as “the most pressing international crisis”.Condemning the destruction and killings at the hands of Israeli forces in Palestine, he said, “We are witnessing the intensification of expansionist policies by the Israeli regime in the West Bank and occupied Al-Quds.”“This is a moment that calls for concrete action, collective responsibility, and an end to silence and indifference.”He concluded his speech by reiterating that Iran’s stability and prosperity were “intrinsically linked” to those of other ECO members.ECO delegation heads call on PM ShehbazSeparately, the foreign ministers and delegation heads of ECO member states paid a joint call on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, according to a handout issued by the PM’s Office.The premier thanked them for their participation in the meeting and reaffirmed Pakistan’s “strong commitment” to ECO objectives. He reiterated his government’s resolve to promote regional cooperation, connectivity and economic integration within the ECO member states.The premier appreciated the meeting’s successful conclusion and welcomed the adoption of the Islamabad Communique and the Strategic Goals of Economic Cooperation 2035, describing them as “important steps” towards strengthening the organisation and advancing shared regional priorities.The premier highlighted Pakistan’s ECO chairmanship and emphasised the need to translate the organisation’s collective vision into concrete, result-oriented initiatives that deliver “tangible benefits” to the region’s people.Furthermore, the handout said that the premier called for enhanced cooperation in trade and investment, transport and transit connectivity, energy, information and communication technology, and sustainable development.“He stressed the importance of effective implementation of existing ECO agreements and strengthening institutional mechanisms to accelerate regional economic integration,” the statement said.PM Shehbaz highlighted the country’s strategic geographical location. He reiterated Pakistan’s commitment to enhancing regional connectivity through road, rail and multimodal transport corridors, including linkages with the ports of Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar, to facilitate access to regional and international markets, particularly for landlocked ECO member states.“Underlining Pakistan’s commitment to dialogue and diplomacy for the peaceful resolution of disputes, the premier stressed the importance of collective efforts to address threats to regional security,” the statement added.He also expressed Pakistan’s resolve to work closely with all member states and the ECO secretariat to further strengthen the organisation during its chairmanship.“The prime minister reaffirmed that Pakistan looked forward to welcoming ECO member states again in 2027 for the next Council of Ministers Meeting and the ECO summit,” the handout concluded.Dar holds sideline meetings with participating dignitariesThe deputy premier also held separate meetings with ministers from several countries attending the ECO moot.WithFM Araghchi, Dar emphasised that dialogue and diplomacy remain the only viable means of addressing outstanding issues, preventing escalation and achieving lasting peace and stability, the Foreign Office said.Meanwhile, Tajikistan’s FM Sirojiddin Muhriddin and Dar reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation within ECO and advancing its regional priorities.According to FO, the Tajik minister appreciated Pakistan’s warm hospitality.The two leaders “underscored the importance of realising the full potential of bilateral trade” and also discussed advancing energy cooperation, particularly through the early operationalisation ofCASA-1000.Dar and Turkiye’s Deputy FM Musa Kulaklikaya reaffirmed their “commitment to further strengthening the longstanding bonds of friendship and brotherhood” between their countries, FO said.Dar thanked Türkiye for its active participation in the Council of Ministers meeting, while Kulaklikaya thanked Pakistan for the warm hospitality and arrangements for the meeting.In his meeting with Dar, Kyrgyz Republic’s Deputy FM Kairat Tursunkulov delivered a letter from Foreign Minister Zheenbek Kulubaev, “reaffirming the close bonds of friendship and commitment to advancing bilateral ties”, FO said.The two sides discussed strengthening bilateral cooperation, particularly in trade and connectivity, and emphasised the importance of continued cooperation under ECO.Pakistan calls on Afghanistan to address terror concernsIn his opening speech at the meeting, Dar said Pakistan desired a peaceful, prosperous and stableAfghanistan, but meaningful progress towards regional cooperation required the Afghan authorities to address the legitimate security concerns of neighbouring countries, particularly the threat of terrorism.He added that a stable Afghanistan, at peace with itself and all its neighbours and fully integrated into the ECO framework, would benefit the Afghan people as well as the wider region by opening up avenues for trade, transit and economic cooperation.“At the same time, meaningful progress requires the Afghan authorities to address the legitimate security concerns of the neighbouring countries, particularly the threat of terrorism,” Dar said.He stressed that a secure and stable environment was essential for sustained regional economic partnerships, adding that these considerations remained central to Pakistan’s broader connectivity agenda.“Regional connectivity rests on more than the routes that link us. It depends upon trust between states and confidence that international commitments will be honoured. Unresolved disputes and the non-fulfilment of international obligations can erode that trust and impede economic progress,” said Dar.The foreign minister emphasised that respect for international law and treaties is essential to enduring economic partnerships between countries.Outlining Pakistan’s priorities during its chairmanship of the ECO, Dar identified five key areas of focus, including expanding trade and investment, strengthening regional connectivity, advancing the ECO Trade Agreement, building regional resilience and promoting human development.The foreign minister said the region’s natural resources, energy reserves, agricultural potential and strategic location offered considerable opportunities for economic cooperation, but realising that potential required functioning transport corridors, efficient border procedures and predictable transit arrangements.He said Pakistan would work towards wider market access, stronger regional value chains and greater private sector participation, particularly by small and medium-sized enterprises, to boost trade and investment among member states.“Closer interaction among our business communities can help translate commercial potential into greater trade and investment.”Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar in a cordial exchange with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Tajikistan Foreign Minister Sirojiddin Muhriddin, OIC Secretary General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed and ECO Secretary General Dr. Asad Majeed Khan on the sidelines of the 30th ECO Council of Ministers Meeting in Islamabad on Nov 16. — ForeignOfficePk/XOn connectivity, Dar said Pakistan would seek to improve transport and transit links between Central Asia, South Asia and Pakistani ports on the Arabian Sea. Harmonised customs procedures, efficient border management and predictable transit arrangements were essential to making regional trade routes commercially viable, he added.The foreign minister also highlighted the need to advance the ECO Trade Agreement, saying the negotiating strategy and roadmap approved by ECO trade ministers in November 2025 provided a basis for modernising the agreement. Pakistan would support efforts to develop a more effective, inclusive and digitally enabled regional trade framework, he said.On regional resilience, Dar called for closer cooperation in disaster preparedness, early warning systems, sustainable water management and climate-resilient infrastructure, noting that climate change and growing pressure on water and energy resources posed serious challenges to regional economies.He also underscored the importance of human development, particularly in education, research, innovation and vocational training, saying greater opportunities in these areas could equip young people with skills needed by changing economies. Promoting entrepreneurship and professional exchanges would further strengthen regional integration, he added.The foreign minister maintained that the five priorities were interconnected and their success would depend on collective efforts by member states. He expressed Pakistan’s readiness to work with ECO members and the organisation’s secretariat on initiatives relating to trade facilitation, transit connectivity and disaster preparedness.Regional peace and diplomatic effortsDar cautioned that peace and stability were essential for economic development, warning that conflict and insecurity in the region could disrupt trade routes, energy supplies, investment and economic projects.“Peace and development reinforce each other,” he said.He added that Pakistan remained “deeply concerned about conflict and instability” in the region.“Their consequences extend beyond national boundaries, disrupting trade routes, energy supplies, investment, and the economic projects of our peoples.”He said that Pakistan has consistently advocated for “the peaceful resolution of disputes through dialogue and diplomacy in accordance with international law and the United Nations Charter”.Referring to Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts in the US-Israeli war on Iran, Dar said, “Pakistan will continue these diplomatic efforts in support of dialogue, de-escalation, and lasting regional stability.”He said that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir “remained closely engaged with brotherly countries and international partners to facilitate peaceful outcomes”.Senior officials meet to finalise agendaSenior officials of the ECO finalised the agenda and draft Islamabad Communiqué on Sunday, ahead of the organisation’s COM meeting.According to a statement issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA), the Senior Officials Meeting (SOM) was held on Nov 15 under the chairmanship of Foreign Secretary Ambassador Asim Iftikhar Ahmad.The meeting was attended by senior officials from ECO member states, representatives of the ECO Secretariat, and delegates from the organisation’s specialised agencies and regional institutions.The officials reviewed preparations for the ministerial meeting and finalised its agenda and the draft Islamabad Communiqué for consideration by the foreign ministers.They also reviewed the activities undertaken by the ECO Secretariat during the year, including ongoing programmes and initiatives, outcomes of sectoral ministerial meetings, and the work of subsidiary bodies and specialised institutions, the ministry said.Administrative and financial matters of the organisation also came under discussion, with participants exchanging views on measures to improve its effectiveness.The SOM serves as a preparatory forum for the ECO COM, enabling member states to assess progress, discuss issues of mutual interest and build consensus on proposals and draft documents ahead of ministerial-level deliberations.

headline: Govt reduces petrol, diesel prices by Rs2 per litre
content: The government on Monday reduced the price of both petrol and high-speed diesel by Rs2 per litre, marking the tenthconsecutivedecrease in the rates. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs328 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs358 on Nov 17 (Tuesday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra). The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. Under anarrangementannounced on Nov 2, for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end. On Sept 17, the governmentrolled outthePrime Minister’s Fuel Relief Schemeacross the country to ease the public’s burden amid rising fuel prices due to the Middle East situation. The subsidy scheme applies to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc. The price of HSD has come down from apeak of Rs520.35recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28. The petrol price hadpeaked at Rs458.41on April 3 after beginning itsupward trajectoryfrom Rs266 in the first week of March. Meanwhile, the government hasreintroduceda raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months. SinceJuly 17, the government has been revising fuel prices on a near-daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Prior to this, the government had been announcingweekly revisionsto fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the conflict. The federal government had alsoannouncedtargeted relief measures in April to provide subsidised fuel. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

headline: Financing for export sector raised to Rs1.5tr
summary: ISLAMABAD: The government has raised financing under the Export Finance Scheme (EFS) to Rs1.5 trillion from Rs1 trillion, with Rs300 billion earmarked for small and medium enterprises and new exporters, as it seeks to drive export-led growth. The revised schemes, which take effect on Nov 1, were reviewed at a meeting held at the Ministry of Finance on Monday.The meeting assessed progress on the SME financing initiative, under which eligible SMEs can now apply for funding through the State Bank of Pakistan’s SME Connect Portal.Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb chaired the review meeting, which was attended by several federal ministers and secretaries of various divisions. The meeting reviewed financing opportunities for SMEs, with a particular focus on the SME Connect Portal and initiatives to enhance access to finance for SME exporters.To support SMEs, the government has also increased the collateral-free financing limit from Rs10 million to Rs50 million. Outstanding SME financing rose from Rs691bn in June 2025 to Rs1.114tr in June 2026, and reached Rs1.148tr by October.Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has set a target of Rs2.2tr by 2028 for the SMEs. Other milestones are SBP’s target of Rs1.5tr by June 2027 and the finance ministry’s target of Rs2tr by June 2028.Govt allocates Rs300bn for SMEsThe government also aims to increase SME borrowers from about 350,862 in September to 775,000 by June 2028.An official announcement said the finance minister underscored the importance of expanding access to finance for SMEs, recognising their contribution to economic activity, investment, and job creation.He emphasised the need to ensure that financing reaches a wider segment of businesses, particularly smaller and export-oriented enterprises.The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) gave a presentation on the progress of the SME Connect Portal, launched on Nov 1, highlighting its role in facilitating access to financing and improving transparency in the application process.The portal provides a central platform for SMEs to register their business profiles, submit their financing requirements and track the status of their requests. It also enables the monitoring of banks’ responses and processing timelines.The minister emphasised that the portal would improve visibility into the financing process and enable systematic monitoring of banks’ performance against prescribed timelines.Published in Dawn, November 17, 2026

headline: Equities post modest gains despite profit-taking
summary: KARACHI: The Pakis­tan Stock Exchange (PSX) opened the week cautiously, with market sentiment mixed on Monday. The benchmark KSE-100 index nevertheless posted modest gains, as profit-taking in the closing hours pared its earlier advances.Topline Securities Ltd said the benchmark remained volatile throughout the session, touching an intraday high of 179,692.98 and a low of 178,065.73, reflecting mixed investor sentiment and intermittent profit-taking. Extending the positive momentum from the weekend session, the index settled at 178,182.95, up 309.07 points, or 0.17 per cent.Market sentiment remained positive after a strong start, with buying interest across key sectors, including oil and gas exploration, cement, and commercial banks. Index-heavy stocks attracted investor interest, supporting the benchmark despite profit-taking during the session.Mari Energies, Hub Power, Engro Holdings, Pakistan Services and Bank Al-Habib emerged as the leading positive contributors, collectively adding approximately 430 points to the benchmark index and providing substantial support to the market’s overall performance. Conversely, Meezan Bank, Fauji Fertiliser, Adamjee Insurance Company Ltd, Fauji Cement Company and Habib Bank were the major laggards, cumulatively eroding 265 points.Ali Najib, Deputy Head of Trading at Arif Habib Ltd, said the PSX surged over 1,500 points during the initial minutes and maintained a positive bias for most of the session.The positive sentiment was underpinned by easing geopolitical tensions and improving global oil supply prospects. Crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz approached pre-conflict levels, while the IEA projected a Q4 supply surplus, easing concerns about prolonged supply disruptions.On the corporate front, Hub Power announced an agreement with a prominent Chinese design institute to conduct a bankable feasibility study and prepare the related report for its proposed aluminium smelter project, which envisages an annual production capacity of 300,000 tonnes.Investor participation remained robust, with trading volume jumping 28.45pc to 1.33 billion shares and total traded value rising 5.1pc to Rs32.58bn. WorldCall Telecom topped the volume chart with over 376 million shares.Analysts expect the market to maintain its positive bias as geopolitical tensions ease and global oil supply prospects improve.Volatility and profit-taking near the 180,000 resistance level may continue, while selective buying in fundamentally strong stocks remains the preferred strategy.Published in Dawn, November 17, 2026

headline: SBP says inflation to ease to 5-7pc target range during FY2027
summary: The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) said on Monday that consumer price inflation was expected to gradually ease towards the medium-term target range of five to seven per cent during financial year 2027.Real GDP growth would remain in the range of 3.5-4.5pc, the bank said in a yearly report, which added the country’s current account deficit was likely to be in the range of 0-1pc of GDP in the financial year.It projected the fiscal deficit to range between 3-4pc of GDP.In its Annual Report on the State of Pakistan’s Economy for FY26, the central bank said Pakistan’s economy demonstrated resilience against domestic and global shocks, with improvements across key macroeconomic indicators during the outgoing fiscal year.According to a statement, the report attributed the gains to a prudent monetary policy stance, continued fiscal consolidation and economic reforms under the International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme, which helped preserve macroeconomic stability despite external and domestic challenges, including shifting US trade tariff policies,monsoon floodingand the outbreak ofconflict in the Middle Eastin February 2026.The statement said real GDP growth increased during FY26, with a major impetus coming from a rebound in large-scale manufacturing. It said the recovery in economic activity led to an increase in imports, while unfavourable global economic trends constrained exports.However, strong growth in workers’ remittances kept the current account deficit at 0.1pc of GDP in FY26. Foreign exchange purchases by the SBP, a reduction in forward liabilities and sustained official inflows also contributed to an improvement in the central bank’s foreign exchange reserves, it added.The statement said continued fiscal consolidation and a substantial decline in interest payments contributed to improved fiscal outcomes during FY26. Prudent monetary and fiscal policies also helped keep average national consumer price inflation close to the upper limit of the medium-term target range of 5-7pc, despite anenergy price shockthat pushed year-on-year inflation into double digits from April 2026 onwards.However, the statement stressed that deep-rooted structural reforms were necessary to place the economy on a sustainable high-growth path and create employment opportunities for the expanding working-age population.A chapter in the report, titled ‘Structural Challenges to Job Creation in Pakistan’, identified weak and volatile economic growth, slow structural transformation and signs of premature deindustrialisation as major obstacles to employment generation.Low female labour force participation, high youth unemployment and widespread informal employment further compound these challenges, the statement said.It added that the report also highlighted emerging pressures from technological developments, the green transition and geoeconomic fragmentation.It called for measures to encourage private sector investment, address infrastructure gaps, improve technology and skills development, rationalise taxes and simplify tax administration. Reducing economic policy uncertainty through rules-based fiscal and regulatory frameworks is also identified as essential for sustained growth.On the macroeconomic outlook, the SBP said Pakistan entered FY27 on a relatively stronger footing, with improvements in key economic indicators also contributing to upgrades in the country’s sovereign credit ratings.A gradual recovery in domestic demand and recent fiscal measures were expected to support economic activity. While worseningEl Niño conditionsposed risks to the agricultural outlook, preliminary information indicated higher output of keykharif crops, including sugarcane, rice and maize, compared to last year, it said.The report expected economic expansion, tariff rationalisation and higher global commodity prices to drive import growth, while exports were projected to recover moderately on the back of policy incentives and a slight increase in global demand.Continued growth in workers’ remittances was expected to keep the current account deficit within 0-1pc of GDP in FY27. Meanwhile, foreign exchange purchases, official inflows and$3 billion raised through Eurobondissuance in September 2026 were expected to support further reserve accumulation towards four months of import cover.The impact of the global energy price shock was expected to put upward pressure on inflation, which was projected to gradually ease towards the medium-term target range of 5-7pc during FY27.

headline: PM Shehbaz approves facilitation centres for SMEs at district level
summary: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Monday approved the establishment of facilitation centres for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) at the district level, with pilot projects in Lahore, Peshawar, Karachi and Quetta.The development came as a delegation of exporters called on the premier, according to the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO). The statement said that during the meeting, progress on measures taken by the government for the promotion of SMEs and their issues were discussed.According to the handout, PM Shehbaz said that SMEs were the “backbone of the country’s economy”.“Providing facilities to increase exports of SMEs is the government’s top priority,” he said, adding that the purpose of the meeting was to create ease in exports for business owners.“In this regard, all measures should be taken to raise awareness among the public regarding establishing businesses,” he said.The handout said that the premier approved SME facilitation centres at district level, ordering that pilot projects be initiated in Lahore, Peshawar, Karachi and Quetta.“The prime minister said that following the success of these facilitation centres, they will be gradually established across all districts so that awareness regarding establishing businesses can be provided to the maximum number of citizens,” the statement said.Furthermore, the premier directed that a plan for establishing a sustainable cold storage system for exporting perishable goods be presented as soon as possible. The statement further said that Rs300 billion had been allocated under the Export Finance Scheme for the SME sector and new exporters.“The allocated funds will be exclusively reserved for SMEs. In this regard, Exim Bank has issued a circular,” he said.He added that approval had also been granted to restructure the Trade Development Authority of Pakistan (TDAP) and Small and Medium Enterprises Development Authority (Smeda) along “modern lines” to promote Pakistani exports and bring local industries in line with export standards.Meanwhile, the delegation’s participants praised the government’s measures to promote small and medium-sized businesses, according to the statement, while presenting proposals for further promoting such enterprises.“The prime minister formed a committee to consider the delegation’s actionable proposals and report to him on their implementation,” the statement said.Earlier this month, PM Shehbazdirectedthe finance ministry to address financing constraints faced by SMEs and the housing sector, saying economic growth and employment generation through these sectors were among the government’s top priorities.

headline: Pay gap widening inequality
summary: Top executives in major public, private and multinational companies enjoy lavish compensation packages, often running in tens of millions of rupees a month, alongside perks like exclusive club memberships and paid overseas family holidays.Yet, officials, corporate leaders and regulators remained unconvinced that widening executive-to-worker pay gaps fueled income inequality, entrenched elitism, encouraged corporate extravagance, promoted patronage culture and undermined efficiency by demotivating the workforce.Globally, sustained debate among workers, academics and policymakers has driven demands for corporate pay transparency as a first step towards correcting unfair disparities. Over the past 15 years, six countries, the US, India, UK, Belgium, France and South Africa, have introduced mandatory executive-to-worker pay ratio disclosures for listed companies. Others, including Pakistan, require gender pay gap reporting, while some mandate comparison of pay trends over successive years.CEO-to-worker pay ratio disclosures are increasingly recognised as tools for exposing wage disparities, strengthening transparency and holding corporate boards accountable for executive rewards relative to employee wages and company performance. They enable shareholders, workers, unions and civil society to scrutinise pay inequalities, influence compensation policies and demand better governance. Clear explanations of pay differentials can also address perception of unfairness and ease workplace resentment.Federal Minister for Overseas Pakistanis and Human Resource Development Chaudhry Salik Hussain remarked that any serious consideration of such proposals would first require credible and comprehensive wage data, a clearer understanding of existing pay disparities across sectors and stronger institutional capacity to monitor and enforce compliance. He emphasised that these were essential prerequisites for evidence-based policymaking, enabling authorities to assess both the feasibility and potential implications of introducing greater corporate pay transparency in Pakistan.SECP Chairman Dr Kabir Ahmed Sidhu said the regulator was working to strengthen reporting guidance and compliance mechanisms to ensure that listed companies provide clearer, more consistent and meaningful disclosures for the benefit of all stakeholders. He cited mandatory gender pay-gap reporting as an important step in that direction.A leading economist, speaking anonymously, warned of widening income inequality, citing a Social Policy and Development Centre (SPDC) estimate placing the per capita income ratio of the richest 10pc to the poorest 40pc of households at 2.3, marking a 21.7pc increase from 2018-19. The actual gap, he argued, is considerably wider as wealthy households underreport earnings while capital gains from property and shares and dividend income largely escape household surveys. Tax records could reveal the true extent of inequality, provided the data is accessible.Prominent business leader Musadaq Zulqarnain questioned the relevance of comparing a handful of top executives’ pay with average worker wages, favouring instead a comparison of senior management compensation with employee earnings. He estimated Pakistan’s ratio at 25:1 to 50:1, which he considered not particularly concerning.“The real concern is that millions of workers in Pakistan’s semi-documented and undocumented sectors are denied even the statutory minimum wage. Correcting this injustice deserves far greater priority,” he argued.Majyd Aziz, president of the Employers Federation of Pakistan, supported fairer corporate pay structures, questioning the widening gap between executive compensation and ordinary workers’ wages. He said disparities were particularly pronounced in multinationals, financial institutions and some state-owned enterprises, where executive remuneration could be disproportionately high.Aziz argued that the debate in Pakistan should focus on total compensation, including perks and privileges often omitted from disclosed salary packages and annual reports.Citing the US, he criticised exorbitant CEO compensation even in loss-making companies facing legal and regulatory challenges. In contrast, Scandinavian countries generally followed more restrained compensation practices.Recalling discussions with multinational executives, Aziz said their hefty packages were justified partly by managerial competence but, more importantly, by their influence in Islamabad and government circles. He questioned whether such influence, rather than performance, warranted extraordinary rewards, particularly when companies continued facing labour disputes and substantial legal expenses.Responding to queries, a spokesperson for the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) reaffirmed the regulator’s commitment to greater pay transparency and equity in listed companies.He said a circular by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP), issued on April 10, 2024, requires listed companies to disclose gender pay gap in their annual reports and on their websites for financial years ending on or after June 30, 2024. The disclosures are also publicly accessible through SECP’s ESG Sustain Portal, bringing Pakistan closer to international standards of corporate transparency and accountability.The spokesperson said further initiatives were planned to strengthen implementation, improve reporting consistency and promote equitable remuneration across organizations. However, he acknowledged that a compliance audit had yet to be conducted.Information gathered suggests that Pakistan’s highest-paid corporate executives, particularly CEOs and presidents of major commercial banks and state-owned financial institutions, draw fixed monthly salaries ranging from Rs9.5 million to over Rs15m. Including performance bonuses, perks and other benefits, their annual compensation packages often exceed Rs300m–400m.Among the highest earners are heads of public-sector and joint-venture financial institutions, including Pak-Kuwait, Pak-Oman, Pak-Iran and Pak-Libya investment companies, and the National Bank of Pakistan. Senior executives of leading private and Islamic banks also command substantial packages.The elite pay bracket extends to top executives in consumer goods, cement, textiles, chemicals, energy, petroleum, tobacco, fertiliser, telecom, media, technology and insurance.Industry observers, however, point out that these headline figures represent gross compensation, with Pakistan’s highest income tax rates substantially reducing executives’ take-home earnings.Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, November 16th, 2026

headline: Pakistan’s private equity needs fixing more than capital
summary: The Saudi–Pakistan private equity fund, launched on Nov 9 with a reported first-phase target of $500 million, 75pc of it earmarked for Pakistan, is a welcome expression of confidence. But it raises a fundamental question: is Pakistan ready for private equity? Capital is only one ingredient. Investible businesses, willing owners, transparent accounts, enforceable shareholder rights and credible exits matter equally, and Pakistan is weak in all of them. The fund may find that raising capital is easier than deploying it profitably, and exiting harder still.Private equity differs from lending or portfolio investment: it acquires stakes, improves performance and sells at a profit. That requires businesses willing to accept outside shareholders, professional management and transparency.Pakistan has no shortage of entrepreneurs, but few businesses are institutionally investible. Ownership is concentrated in families reluctant to dilute control, share decisions or accept scrutiny. Reporting and governance standards vary widely, and transparency may expose undocumented transactions and tax liabilities.Yet genuine needs exist. Succession disputes, retiring founders, expansion plans and heirs unwilling to run inherited businesses create openings for outside capital. Minority stakes can finance growth without displacing families; majority acquisitions can give owners an exit. Both sides need protection: investors require enforceable rights over major decisions, related-party transactions and exits; families need assurance against unrealistic performance demands and premature sales.The most promising opportunity is consolidation. Textiles, engineering and food processing contain many firms too small to achieve scale, invest in technology or meet international standards. Private equity could combine them into professionally managed enterprises able to compete globally.Private equity needs clarity on the taxation of income, dividends, capital gains, restructuring and distributions. Taxing the same income at company, fund and investor levels would erode returns. Tax-neutral mergers and share exchanges, predictable capital gains treatment and relief from cascading dividend taxation would help, as would pass-through taxation, with safeguards against disguising ordinary business income as concessionally taxed gains. The National Private Equity Framework, still being drafted, is the right vehicle. Its reforms should benefit all qualifying investors, not only participants in this initiative.The recent super tax cuts, including exemption for large exporters, are a welcome correction. But high corporate and dividend taxation and uncertain treatment of restructuring still deter investment.Pakistan’s greatest weakness may be the absence of reliable exits. The Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) offers few sizable listings; concentrated ownership, limited free float and compliance costs discourage companies from going public. Strategic buyers are few, and sales back to founders depend on their liquidity.Abraaj’s experience is a warning. Shanghai Electric agreed in 2016 to buy its controlling stake in K-Electric for $1.77 billion; the deal was abandoned in 2025. Abraaj’s own collapse compounded concerns about fund governance, though not every difficulty was its doing: K-Electric’s regulated business, circular debt and government disputes created separate complications. The lesson is plain nonetheless: an investor may acquire an asset yet struggle for years to leave it.Private equity cannot flourish where contracts are hard to enforce, approvals unpredictable and repatriation uncertain. Pakistan needs credible pathways to IPOs, strategic sales and buybacks, backed by effective commercial dispute resolution.The test should be whether investment is productive rather than speculative: does it add employment, productivity and export earnings, not merely transaction value? By that test, consolidation of established industries stands out. Agriculture offers dairy, meat processing, horticulture, cold chains and food exports, where Saudi partners could bring assured markets. Auto components have developed valuable engineering skills; consolidation could improve scale and quality and enable diversification into electric vehicle parts, agricultural machinery and industrial equipment. Export-oriented textiles, pharmaceuticals, surgical instruments and established IT exporters offer similar scope.Other candidates suit conventional private equity less. Mining needs specialist expertise and patient capital. Railways, ports and airports have long horizons and regulatory risks are better served by dedicated infrastructure vehicles. Monetising government land may yield immediate proceeds without creating productive capacity, and deserves caution.Foreign investors measure returns in dollars. A business earning 15pc in rupees delivers only about 4.5pc in dollars if the rupee depreciates 10pc a year. That strengthens the case for export-oriented investments over businesses reliant on protected domestic markets.Fund governance is equally important: transparent decisions, independent valuations, conflict-of-interest safeguards and professional management. Deals involving businesses linked to sponsors need particularly rigorous scrutiny, and improving performance after investment demands specialist knowledge across sectors.The government’s role is to improve tax rules, shareholder protection, listing opportunities, repatriation procedures and commercial dispute resolution, and to avoid guarantees or privileges that shift investment risks to taxpayers.The $500m remains a target, not committed capital, and success should be judged by more than money deployed. The real test is whether the fund creates additional investment rather than merely transferring ownership, improves governance, consolidates fragmented enterprises, generates exports and jobs, and builds a record of successful exits.Pakistan needs long-term risk capital, but capital cannot overcome weak governance, unpredictable policy and an underdeveloped market for corporate ownership. The initiative could catalyse change; its greatest contribution may be showing that transparent, internationally competitive businesses can attract capital without protection or privilege.Pakistan’s challenge is not simply to attract private equity. It is to create enterprises worthy of investment, and a market from which investors can eventually exit.The author is a former CEO of Unilever Pakistan and of the Pakistan Business Council.Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, November 16th, 2026

headline: Fertiliser sector — Hopes and hurdles
summary: Pakistan’s fertiliser sector enters the closing months of 2026 on a cautiously optimistic note. The outlook for urea is somewhat stronger than that for phosphatic fertilisers. Domestic nitrogenous fertiliser demand has shown signs of recovery but persistent weakness in diammonium phosphate (DAP) offtake reflects mounting affordability constraints being faced by farmers.According to the National Fertiliser Development Centre (NFDC), urea sales rose by 8.4pc during the Kharif season while DAP offtake declined by 25.4pc. The forthcoming Rabi season, particularly wheat sowing, is expected to support industry volumes. The Ministry of National Food Security and Research estimates urea demand at 3.596m tonnes and DAP requirements at 838,000 tonnes.The sector’s principal strength is its substantial domestic manufacturing base, which offers some protection against international price volatility. Yet dependence on natural gas remains a structural risk. Winter gas load-management measures and uncertainty over liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies could disrupt production at some plants and put pressure on inventories.Elevated DAP prices, subdued farm economics and uncertainty over crop returns are also likely to restrain demand for imported phosphatic fertilisers. The government’s challenge is to ensure adequate supplies without imposing an excessive financial burden on growers.Winter gas outages and uncertainty over LNG supplies could disrupt production at some plants; High DAP prices, subdued farm economics are likely to restrain demand for imported phosphatic fertilisersFor investors, established manufacturers are likely to retain their earnings and dividend appeal, particularly those with favourable gas arrangements, efficient operations and strong market positions. Any improvement in profitability, however, must be weighed against regulatory intervention, feedstock costs and the sustainability of farmers’ purchasing power.For the nine months ending on Sept 30, 2026, major listed fertiliser companies reported year-on-year growth in profit after tax (PAT), with Fauji Fertiliser Company (FFC) leading the group. The FFC posted a consolidated PAT of Rs71bn, up about 13pc from Rs63.04bn in the corresponding period of 2025. Its standalone PAT was approximately Rs64.1bn. The consolidated result reflects the merged operations of the Fauji Fertiliser Bin Qasim (FFBL), which has been absorbed into the FFC and is no longer reported as a separate listed entity. The FFC’s earnings were supported by a 16pc increase in net turnover to Rs373.2bn, driven by higher urea offtake and robust investment income from associates.The Fatima Fertiliser reported consolidated PAT of Rs29.9bn, up about 4pc from Rs28.9bn a year earlier. Despite a 64pc decline in other incomes, the company expanded its gross profit margin to 40pc from 35pc, helping offset higher administrative costs.The Engro Fertilisers posted consolidated PAT of Rs16.2bn, up about 14pc from Rs14.2bn in 9M 2025. Growth was concentrated in the third quarter, when net profit rose 57pc year-on-year to Rs9.1bn, supported by an 11pc increase in net sales and improved gross margins.Pakistan’s fertiliser industry entered the 2000s as a mature, largely deregulated sector. By FY2000, annual production capacity stood at 5.6m tonnes and actual output at 5m tonnes. Urea accounted for 75pc of capacity and 78.4pc of production. Deregulation of urea in 1986 and DAP in 1993, along with duty-free machinery imports and feedstock subsidies, had helped double urea capacity from 2.2m tonnes to 4.3m tonnes by 2000.A pivotal shift came with the Fertiliser Policy of 2001. It formalised market-based pricing, continued concessional gas for qualifying expansion projects and treated capacity debottlenecking on a par with the establishment of new plants. The policy framework, alongside the privatisation of the National Fertiliser Corporation units, encouraged further investment.By 2001, Pakistan had achieved urea self-sufficiency, producing 4.8m tonnes against offtake of 4.2m tonnes. Regular urea imports ended in 2000-01; the country exported 46,000 tonnes in 2002-03. This transition from import dependence to self-sufficiency remains one of the sector’s defining industrial achievements.The success, however, did not extend to phosphates. Between 1998-99 and 2002-03, imports averaged about 11pc of nitrogen deliveries but 72.5pc of phosphate deliveries. Annual phosphate and potash demand of 1.4m tonnes was met entirely through imports, including 1.2m tonnes of DAP. Urea’s achievement was substantial, but the phosphate market remained structurally dependent on overseas supplies.Today, Pakistan has 10 urea plants and a total fertiliser capacity of about 9.4m product tonnes per annum, with urea accounting for roughly 71pc. Urea nameplate capacity exceeds 7m tonnes against average demand of around 6.1m tonnes. During July-March FY2026, fertiliser production reached 7m tonnes, down 0.3pc from the corresponding period a year earlier.The sector’s progress has been driven not only by new investment but also by debottlenecking and efficiency improvements. Urea plants operated at an average utilisation rate of 112pc and DAP at 124pc in 2025, according to industry figures. Such rates reflect output above nominal nameplate capacity and underline the role of operational optimisation.Major listed producers — FFC, Engro Fertilisers and Fatima Fertiliser — now anchor the industry. Merger of the FFBL into the FFC has further consolidated capacity under a single listed entity. The FFC has around 2.6m tonnes per annum of urea nameplate capacity and, through its Port Qasim facility, is Pakistan’s sole domestic DAP producer. Its DAP capacity is somewhere between 670,000 and 800,000 tonnes per annum.Phosphates remain the sector’s weak link. Pakistan produces around 0.7m-0.8m tonnes of DAP against annual demand estimated at 1.2m-1.5m tonnes, leaving a substantial gap to be met through imports. DAP imports reached 620,000 tonnes in 2025, below the average of 835,000 tonnes recorded during 2020-24, but still exposing farmers to international prices and exchange-rate movements.Gas availability is an equally binding constraint. The fertiliser sector consumed 764m cubic feet per day (MMCFD), or 26.1pc of national gas, in FY2025-26. Plants connected to the Sui Northern Gas Pipelines Limited (SNGPL) network have faced repeated shutdowns amid uncertainty over regasified liquefied natural gas (RLNG) supplies. Production interruptions have threatened substantial urea output, with some industry estimates indicating a potential loss of 718,000 tonnes by September 2026.The industry’s self-sufficiency in urea therefore rests on reliable and affordable gas supplies. Any prolonged disruption can erode the gains achieved through decades of investment and efficiency improvements. Meanwhile, the absence of comparable domestic capacity in phosphates leaves farmers exposed to imported fertiliser prices at a time when farm incomes and purchasing power are under pressure and rural poverty is on the rise.Published in Dawn, The Business and Finance Weekly, November 16th, 2026
