headline: No casualties reported as huge blaze engulfs industrial unit in Karachi's Baldia Town
summary: KARACHI: A massive fire broke out at an industrial unit in Karachi’s Baldia Town on Tuesday morning, reportedly during the refilling of an underground oil tank by a tanker, rescue officials said.The fire that erupted in the morning was controlled in the afternoon by over a dozen fire tenders after hectic efforts, lasting for several hours; however, no casualties were reported.Site-B police said that the fire broke out in a plastic factory at Rasheedabad. Rescue 1122 spokesperson Hassaanul Haseeb Khan toldDawnthat the fire had broken out in a factory that manufactured glass products.The rescue official said that information regarding the fire was first received at 10:36am. He said that initially two fire tenders were sent to the scene, but more were later dispatched due to the severity of the blaze.The spokesperson added that the factory was housed in a two-storey building and manufactured glass products, including windowpanes and decorative items.“During the preliminary probe, it emerged that an oil tanker was refilling an underground oil tank when it caught fire and exploded,” the spokesperson said.The explosion caused oil to spread both inside the factory premises and onto nearby streets, triggering panic among firefighters and residents, he elaborated. He said 11 fire tenders, with the help of two snorkels and two disaster vehicles, managed to control the fire at around 3:45pm.The rescue official said that the fire had spread from the ground floor to the first and second floors.“All the floors were destroyed along with the raw material that was being stored there. However, the fourth and fifth floors remained unaffected,” he said.Regarding the possible cause of the fire, the Rescue 1122 spokesperson said that it would be ascertained after a thorough probe.In late October, over 30 shops weredestroyedwhen a blaze erupted at a furniture market in Karachi’s Gulistan-i-Jauhar.The fire safety audit of buildings across Karachi has beeninitiated, with 1,369 buildings audited by November 12 in all seven districts of the city.

headline: In hard-hitting speech, Bilawal says system was ‘made to collapse’
summary: Key takeaways:Bilawal opposed creating new provinces ‘unconstitutionally’, such asvia referendum;urged PML-Nto decide on provinces issue, claimed ‘pressure’ on PPPCalled for releasing “political prisoners”,including Imran; noted “injustices” to opposition regarding reserved seats, PTI symbolSaid 27th Amendmentpassed without consensus; supported Fazl’s “right to criticise” govtAmid debate on a “system reset” in the country, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari said on Tuesday that the governance system had not collapsed, but was rather “made to collapse”.Over the past few months, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has whipped up apolitical stormsince he called for the formation ofnew administrative unitsin the country, saying the current “system” of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”.During his speech at the Karachi Press Club, Bilawal recalled Naqvi’s remarks and said, “Nobody objects that the system has collapsed, but there is no discussion and debate on why it collapsed.”He noted that the proposed solution “was not an actual remedy to the illness due to which we suffered a system collapse”.“If we want to focus on resolving the issues of the public, if we want to fight poverty, unemployment, inflation, then we absolutely need to decide why the system collapsed,” the Bhutto scion said.’Reset must be political’Bilawal asserted a reset was “definitely needed”; however, he also stressed that it should be political.“Why political? Because politicians are the representatives of the people, and if politicians do not play their role, then these fundamental issues won’t be resolved,” Bilawal said.“I believe the system has not collapsed, but it has been made to collapse,” he stated, while acknowledging his own role in the matter.“Everyone makes mistakes, but there comes a time when you must fix those mistakes. How do we fix that?” Bilawal asked rhetorically.He contended that state institutions had “lost their legitimacy”, calling for it to be restored.During his speech at the ‘Meet the Press’ event and responding to queries later, Bilawal firmly declared that the PPP would oppose any “unconstitutional” moves regarding new provinces.He also voiced his strong opposition to a referendum on creating new provinces, questioning the “intent” behind it, and said his party lawmakers were facing “pressure” but would not succumb to it.The PPP chairman’s remarks went beyond his oft-repeated calls for electoral reforms and political consensus, as he called for the opposition PTI to be given reserved seats as a “confidence-building measure”.He also questioned the current status of the judiciary, particularly in the wake of the 27th Amendment, which he had stronglyadvocatedfor at the time of its passage just a year ago.‘Injustices’ to PTI of reserved seats, symbolThe PPP chairman further observed that “some such injustices” had been done that, if corrected, could quickly restore the opposition’s trust.In an indirect reference to thePTI, Bilawal recalled the revocation of the PPP’s party symbol in 1988 and said, “Revoking the symbol from a party is akin to you joking with the public, and the public denounced this tradition and action and responded to you in those elections.”Then, in a stance deviating from the ruling coalition’s, Bilawal said that “what happened with the reserved seats was a joke”. He said the opposition was not only deprived of those seats, but “those in the treasury benches also put them in their pockets”.The PTI —deprivedof itsreserved seatsin the 2024 elections — wasdeclared eligiblefor the seats by the Supreme Court. However, a constitutional bench formed later via the 26th Amendmentoverturnedthat ruling while hearing review pleas of the coalition parties.“And from those same reserved seats, which are not yours, you brought constitutional amendments not once but twice, and are now thinking to bring a third one,” Bilawal said.He called for resolving reservations regarding rigging and returning the party symbol “so they have their own identity”.“It is a confidence-building measure that we, without any preconditions, return the reserved seats to the opposition, which is their right,” said Bilawal, whose PPP was alsoamong the beneficiariesof the reserved seats case.‘Imran Khan a political prisoner’Reiterating his call for electoral reforms, Bilawal also stressed the need to restore the PTI’s and the opposition’s trust in the Parliament.“If we want the system to be reset and the Parliament to start functioning, vengeful actions will need to be stopped. How much revenge will you take after all?” he said.The PPP chairman said not only should vengeful actions be halted, but the “tradition of revenge inserted in Pakistan’s politics” should be ended forever.He even recalled a speech by PTI founder Imran Khan, who questioned if “we were ants”.Bilawal called for efforts to ensure that there is no political prisoner in Pakistan, terming it necessary for the “system to function”.“What a weird country this is; since 1947, whoever becomes the prime minister goes to jail, whoever gets out of jail goes to sit in the Prime Minister House,” he remarked.“You broke [our] back, then ask ‘why did you fall’,” he quipped, emphasising that political prisoners would need to be released.When asked whether he considered Imran a political prisoner, Bilawal responded in the affirmative.“A person becomes the prime minister and is later imprisoned. So I can either accept that every prime minister in the country’s history has been a thief, or I can accept that all prime ministers in our history have been victims of political revenge,” he added.Noting that the PTI had made mistakes as well, Bilawal said, “One day, I hope no prime minister should have to go to jail, and for that, we need to develop consensus.”‘Federal govt must decide on reset’Bilawal, in response to a question, also called on the federal government to present its stance on the governance reset.Presenting his own approach, he said, “The political reset that I spoke of, I will try to develop that consensus, and I would like to create a consensus for it in my own party so that we can engage other political parties”.As for the federal government, Bilawal said, “I don’t know what they are thinking.”In an apparent reference to the interior minister’s remarks about being on the “same page” as Bilawal, the PPP chairman said, “I had heard we were on the same page, and if this is the page we are on, then nothing could be better.”Bilawal said there had been a debate that had been “forced” in the country for the past few months.“Even the cabinet had not discussed the matter, let alone the parliament [..] So, how could it be that federal ministers are talking about it of their own accord,” he asked.At this, the PPP chairman said he would like to believe that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has “enough authority over his own ministers”.“You are sabotaging your own prime minister, and then you complain that the system has collapsed [..] I believe that is unfair.”In recent days, PML-N’s Khawaja Asif, who serves as the defence minister, has beenadvocatingfor new administrative units,suggestingthe formation of up to 12 provinces.Bilawal maintained that his party would welcome any debate and consensus on the matter; however, he hinted that deliberation and consensus “may not be on the agenda”.Bilawal said that “suggestions” were coming from outside of the Parliament, which he described as showing “clear indication [..] that the opinion of Parliament, public, and cabinet did not hold any weight and you just want to use a backdoor channel”.“Up until today, neither the prime minister nor a single member of the provinces has brought up the issue with the president of Pakistan or me,” he added.On a possible rollback of the 18th Amendment, Bilawal pointed out that the Sindh government was giving the Centre Rs585 billion surplus in financial support.“Donations worth Rs 260bn were given in security and national interest,” he said.“I am not even counting the rightful share of the province — of petroleum levy and gas levy — it is about Rs1.7 trillion from the petroleum levy.”He remarked, “So, you will pickpocket the province, loot our resources and then come and ask us, ‘why the roads are broken and why no schools or hospitals have been built’.”Bilawal assailed the Centre, asking if a province was paying a Rs585bn surplus, Rs260bn for national security and Rs1.7tr on the petroleum levy, then “the federal government should be held responsible for the lack of public spending, not the provincial government”.He claimed that the “easiest way to do corruption in Pakistan was to be on the state’s right side”.‘Referendum has never been democratic’On the interior minister’srecommendationof holding a referendum to decide on the creation of administrative units, the PPP chairman pointed to the “intention” behind the proposed action.“In our history, a referendum has always been carried out for an undemocratic act and never a democratic one,” the Bhutto scion remarked.He argued that if the Constitution had relevant provisions on the creation of administrative units, then the mere suggestion of holding a referendum “meant that you were looking for an unconstitutional method”.The PPP chairman vowed that his party would stand firmly against any such “unconstitutional” action.Bilawal also spoke against “any forced division” in Sindh, warning that while PPP remained in favour of creating provinces, it was against a “forced separation”.He cautioned, “We talk about the garbage on Karachi’s streets, but if Sindh is divided, we will see blood flow through its streets.”On being asked whether a compromise could be reached on the creation of new provinces, Bilawal recalled that several resolutions had been passed by the Sindh Assembly against the province’s division.“Any more discussion on this issue is a slap to the people of Sindh,” he declared.“I do not understand what Mohsinbhaiis trying to do,” Bilawal said.Replying to a question about new provinces and a “reset”, Bilawal said the PML-N-led government had not discussed the matter with the PPP, adding that this raised the question of why this was “being made to discuss by the media”.Bilawal said he has invited PM Shehbaz to hold talks with the Sindh government on public issues, and also suggested that he convene his cabinet meetings in each province.‘Pressure on PPP lawmakers’Reiterating the PPP’s stance on new provinces, Bilawal stressed that as a generational politician, he would want to take steps as per the public’s wishes.“Those from whom these suggestions are coming, they have not won even a single election in their lives. And neither do they have chances in the next election … they would become a minister, prime minister or chief minister whether they get a single vote or not in the next elections,” he said, adding that each side was taking a stance as per their situation.Replying to another query, Bilawal said, “On the one hand, there are no discussions ongoing; on the other hand, there definitely is pressure on the party’s MNAs and MPAs, but PPP’s representatives do not function on someone else’s pressure, but the public’s.”He further remarked, “If tomorrow, my software is updated and I direct my party to vote for Sindh’s division, there will be a revolt against me. They will not cast a majority vote even on my directives.”He quipped that “some people were dreaming of becoming the chief minister of their area, but they would not even be able to remain their house’s chief minister”.The Bhutto scion further affirmed that his PPP would not “back any conspiracy against Punjab”, adding that he would support only those decisions endorsed by the Punjab Assembly.He pointed out that there was a lack of discussion on declaring Gilgit-Baltistan a province even though there was a consensus in the region on this demand.‘27th Amendment passed with brute majority’Speaking on the judiciary, Bilawal noted that “our internal wish of a constitutional court” as per the Charter of Democracy had been fulfilled, but questioned whether the court had the public’s confidence.“If the lawyers and judges themselves do not have confidence in the courts, then the system did not collapse, but was made to collapse.”The PPP chairman said he was not calling for the revocation of such moves, but for greater consensus. He asserted that the 26th Amendment was passed with “bilateral agreement, if not complete consensus”, as the opposition’s input was taken through Fazl.Bilawal said the 27th Amendment was “passed neither through political consensus nor bilateral agreement; it was passed with brute majority”.He called for engaging with the opposition on judicial reforms and termed it a requirement for the “political, public and democratic reset”, adding that without such a reset, the public’s key issues of inflation and unemployment cannot be addressed.Bilawal also noted that rigging allegations often surfaced during elections.“I have been in politics for the past 20 years, and usually, I have seen that it is the opposition that accuses the other side of rigging and the government denies it. For the first time, I am seeing that people from within the government are claiming that rigging has been done.”‘Fazl has right to criticise govt’Bilawal also came to Maulana Fazlur Rehman’s defence as tensions between the Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief and the government have flared in recent weeks.The past month has witnessedexchangesofharsh remarksbetween Fazl and federal ministers, after the JUI-F chiefaccusedthe Centre of depriving the provinces of their rights.These developments came after Fazljoinedthe opposition in criticising the Centre’simpositionof governor’s rule and emergency in the PTI-ruled KP. He alsoaccused the Centre of renegingon its commitments amid hisefforts to mediatebetween the federal and KP governments.In his address, Bilawal stressed that it was the opposition’s role in the Parliament to criticise the government.“It is the opposition’s right to criticise you, and however he (Fazl) does it, it is their right,” he said.Bilawal remarked that the opposition had the “most patriotic” role in the Parliament.“For any government to question the patriotism of an opposition member [..] it is not only an injustice to that parliament or to the system, but the biggest injustice to the country,” he added.The PPP chairman termed a difference of opinion within the Parliament the “beauty and strength of democracy”.Bilawal reiterated, “If we want to reset the system, a political reset has to happen; it should begin from the parliament”.He noted that the opposition had lost trust in the system.“They genuinely have reasons to have lost confidence in the working of the Parliament, and we all have to regain this trust,” he said.“The government cannot expect the opposition to clap along with every one of the government’s decisions,” he remarked.He claimed that the “easiest way to do corruption in Pakistan was to be on the state’s right side”.Bilawal said: “When someone from the opposition makes a speech [..] then all of a sudden, you set the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) on them, arrest their sons; there was no such realisation before.“Now, all of a sudden, there is encroachment (around their house),” he said, in an apparent reference to the Capital Development Authority’s (CDA) recent notice on “unauthorised construction” at the JUI-F chief’s residence.“This is why the system has collapsed […] you are making it collapse,” he said, calling on the Centre to engage with Fazl.On governor’s rule in KP, Bilawal noted that PPP had the governor in the province, but stressed his stance that it could not remain forever.“If you are yourself saying that the majority of them (PTI) were ready but one or two people sabotaged the talks, then what is stopping the government from approaching the opposition again?” he said, recalling remarks by “minister for everything”.“If the PTI is ready to fight against terrorism together with you, then the governor’s rule can also be ended,” Bilawal said, terming it another way to regain the opposition’s trust.

headline: FCC directs LDA to stop ‘frivolous litigation’ against family of martyred national hero Rashid Minhas
summary: ISLAMABAD: The Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) has strongly rebuked the Lahore Development Authority (LDA) for prolonging the agony of the family of Pakistan Air Force (PAF) Pilot Officer Rashid Minhas Shaheed, recipient of the country’s highest military gallantry award, Nishan-i-Haider, and directed the authority not to squander its resources and public money on “frivolous, vexatious and obnoxious” litigation against individuals.The observation came in a judgment authored by Justice Ali Baqar Najafi, who regretted that the LDA had continued to drag the family of the martyred officer into litigation over a property dispute.“The family is facing the agony perpetuated by the LDA by dragging them in the courts in frivolous litigation,” the judge observed in the judgment released on Tuesday.Justice Najafi was heading a three-member FCC bench, also comprising Justice Rozi Khan Barrech and Justice Syed Arshad Hussain Shah, which took up an appeal filed by the LDA director general against a March 5, 2018, Lahore High Court (LHC) judgment in favour of Farooq Minhas, the martyred pilot’s real brother.The controversy stemmed from a consent decree passed in favour of Farooq Minhas, the respondent, on May 7, 2005. During subsequent execution proceedings, the LDA objected, arguing that the 14-marla plot in Gulberg-III, Lahore, was evacuee property acquired by the authority for the development of the Gulberg-III scheme.It further maintained that its predecessor, the Lahore Improvement Trust (LIT), had paid the award amount to the custodian of evacuee property and taken physical possession of the land on Dec 24, 1955.The authority also contended that the property fell within the boundaries specified in a notification issued on Aug 6, 1953, and that the award announced by the Land Acquisition Collector on Oct 30, 1962, had been finalised. It argued that no exemption or adjustment had been granted to the respondent’s predecessors-in-interest, Nawab Mirza and Maqsooda Begum.The LDA further questioned Maqsooda Begum’s acquisition of the property through a sale deed dated March 7, 1976, from Nawab Mirza, son of Agha Muhammad Hussain. The latter had claimed ownership on the basis of Property Transfer Document (PTD) No. 213, issued by the Deputy Settlement Commissioner on June 8, 1966, four years after the award was announced on Oct 30, 1962. According to the authority, the transaction was against the policy.However, the FCC noted that the LDA’s objections had consistently been rejected by the executing court, the revisional court and the LHC.Justice Najafi observed that the appeal challenged concurrent findings of the three courts, which had dismissed the authority’s objections during the execution proceedings relating to the May 7, 2005 decree.The court noted that the earlier decisions and the decree had attained finality, particularly as the consent decree had been passed on the basis of the LDA’s own “no objection”.It further observed that a declaration had also been granted in favour of the legal heirs of Maqsooda Begum, while the objections raised under Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) were frivolous and beyond the scope of an executing court.The courts below had also rejected the LDA’s claim that the Central Government had transferred the evacuee portion of the land to the LIT through a notification issued on May 16, 1951, under Section 12 of the Pakistan (Administration of Evacuee Property) Ordinance, 1949. They observed that there was no evidence of such a transfer or of any payment having been made to the LIT or the custodian.The FCC also referred to an Aug 17, 1980 decision of the Vigilance Commission, which stated that duly verified transfer orders would be honoured by the LDA and that only development charges would be recovered from the transferees. The authority had accepted and acted upon the decision, with its director general issuing the necessary directions.The LHC had consequently directed the LDA to stop claiming ownership of the disputed land, which had already become part of the Gulberg-III scheme, the FCC observed.The high court’s judgment was subsequently challenged by the LDA before the Supreme Court, which dismissed the petition, holding that the authority had no ownership rights over the land, as it had already been transferred by the Settlement Department to the occupants. The apex court had also found no reason to interfere with the LHC’s findings.“We, therefore, deem it appropriate that, instead of imposing costs, we direct the Director General, LDA, to ensure that the authority does not deplete its resources or public money on frivolous, vexatious and obnoxious litigation against individuals,” Justice Najafi observed.The FCC dismissed the LDA’s appeal, ruling that it was devoid of merit and refusing leave to appeal.

headline: Bangladesh garment workers, police clash in fresh wage protest
summary: Bangladeshi police fired tear gas and stun grenades on Tuesday in clashes with thousands of garment workers who wereprotestingafter a key wage board meeting was postponed.Protesters hurled bricks, torched vehicles and blocked the main highway between capital Dhaka and key financial district Mymensingh as demonstrations demanding higher wages turned violent.The South Asian nation of 170 million people is the world’s second-biggestgarment exporterbehind China, producing clothes for major international brands including Fruit of the Loom and Levi Strauss.But growing workerunrestover wages that began in October has threatened to disrupt the industry that generates $38 billion in revenues annually and employs more than four million people.Garment workers look on from a bridge during a protest demanding increase in minimum wages, in Gazipur city on the outskirts of Dhaka on November 17, 2026. — AFPWorkers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($240) — a 140-per cent increase on the current 12,500 taka, as they struggle to cope with rising food, housing, transport and healthcare costs.Some 500 factories out of 4,500 are shut, sources toldAFP, something that is further stoking unrest among workers.A “no work, no pay” provision of the country’s labour laws allows factory owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.“The owners seem unwilling to meet our salary demands. They are already dragging their feet,” said Khanom, 24, who gave only one name.Tensions were also running high in the other garment hubs of Savar and Ashulia on the outskirts of Dhaka.The wage board, comprising representatives of employers and workers, was set up by the government earlier this month to negotiate a pay rise.A garment worker throws back a tear gas cannister during a protest demanding increase in minimum wages, in Gazipur city on the outskirts of Dhaka on November 17, 2026. — AFP‘Monitoring cell’The new minimum wage would be announced in December and take effect in January.“We want to return to our machines,” said Rakib, 28, another garment worker.“We are not sure if the wage board members are aware of our demands,” he said, adding that workers feared their concerns might not be reflected in the revised wage proposal.Most factories had opened on Tuesday morning but were shut down as protests spread to the highway, Rakib said.In a joint statement, the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) called for a resumption of wage negotiations as soon as possible.A wage board meeting scheduled for Monday was postponed after a member representing the garment workers said he was unwell, a source in BGMEA toldAFP.The next meeting would be held on November 23, the board said.In the wake of Tuesday’s protest, the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) stepped up patrols across the industrial zone, deploying hundreds of personnel.A garment worker throws back a tear gas cannister during a protest demanding increase in minimum wages, in Gazipur city on the outskirts of Dhaka on November 17, 2026. — AFP“BGB headquarters has been closely observing the situation from a monitoring cell,” it said in a statement.The force said it was also using drones, body-worn cameras and other devices to keep a close watch on demonstrations.The country’s garment industry makes clothes for some of the world’s best-known brands but the sector has been marred by longstanding disputes over wages, working conditions and labour rights.The United States is its biggest individual market, while the European Union is its largest trading bloc.The latest disruption comes during the run-up to Christmas, the busiest export period for Bangladesh’s garment industry.

headline: US releases details of Megaspeed probe, says investigation began in 2024
summary: The US Commerce Department and Justice Department released information on Monday about Washington’s investigation into Singapore-based cloud-computing company Megaspeed, Nvidia’s Asia-Pacific partner, which the departments said began two years ago.Megaspeed has come under scrutiny after reports that Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang had anaffairwith Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, a former top executive at Megaspeed who some US authorities suspect had ties to Chinese espionage efforts.Jensen Huangresignedfrom Nvidia on November 12 andReutershas not been able to contact Alice Huang for comment.“After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations,” the two agencies said in a joint statement.In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed and in June 2025 Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, the joint statement said. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular business hours.US agents, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an “on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed” in June 2025 and interviewed Alice Huang, who was then CEO, the Commerce and Justice Departments said.Following the enforcement action, the Justice Department took the lead role in a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, the statement added.The statement said that while US agencies typically did not comment on ongoing investigations, on this occasion the details provided were in the public interest.US and Singapore discussions on MegaspeedMegaspeed said on Sunday that Alice Huang officially left the company on August 30, 2025, and that it conducted a “legitimate and lawful business.” Singapore’s government said on Monday it had agreed to continue discussions with Washington about Megaspeed.It said last week that Alice Huang had previously worked as the company’s chief executive, chairperson and one of its key controllers.Police found insufficient evidence that she had committed offences relating to suspected false declarations over server purchases, but warned her for knowingly providing inaccurate information that played down her role.The city-state has barred her from re-entering Singapore, while investigations into Megaspeed and six other individuals continue, the home affairs ministry has said.Several news organisations, including theNew York Times, have reported that US and other government authorities had suspicions that Alice Huang was spying for Beijing.Reutershas not been able to verify any of the allegations made in theNew York Times, along with other media reports, about Huang’s suspected espionage.US intelligence agencies are still trying to determine her relationship with China’s Ministry of State Security, according to two sources familiar with the matter.Evidence gathered so far indicated she was probably an intelligence asset, someone who shared information, rather than a fully trained spy, the sources said.Beijing has rejected allegations that Alice Huang is a spy.

headline: New Zealand all-rounder Santner ruled out of India Tests
summary: New Zealand all-rounder and limited-overs captain Mitchell Santner was on Tuesday ruled out of the two-Test series against India after breaking a bone in his hand.Santner was struck while batting during Sunday’s fifth One-day International against India and a scan showed a fracture in his non-bowling right hand.New Zealand host India in Wellington on Thursday to begin a two-Test series which concludes in Christchurch from November 27.It leaves the left-arm spinner doubtful for the subsequent four-Test series in Australia, which begins on December 9 in Perth, eight days after the India series concludes.“Scans have revealed that Santner has fractured his right hand,” said New Zealand Cricket. “His return-to-play timeline is being worked through and his involvement in the Test series in Australia will be updated in due course.”Spin-bowling all-rounder Dean Foxcroft, who made his Test debut against Ireland in May, has replaced Santner in New Zealand’s 14-man Test squad.Spin does not usually play a big role on New Zealand’s seamer-friendly wickets and captain Tom Latham may rely on part-time spinners Glenn Phillips and Rachin Ravindra to back up a four-pronged pace attack.The series will see the two nations meet in red-ball cricket for the first time since New Zealand’s historic 3-0 Test series win in India in 2024.

headline: Pakistan’s pace trio routs Sri Lanka for 98 before hosts take control
summary: Pakistan’s fast bowlers dismissed Sri Lanka for a paltry 98 before the home side reached 121-3 on the opening day of the second Test at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Tuesday, taking a 23-run lead into the close of play.Mohammad Abbas, Razaullah and Aamer Jamal claimed three wickets apiece as Sri Lanka were bowled out in 35.3 overs after Pakistan won the toss and elected to field on a green-tinged pitch.The visitors’ innings was the lowest total by any team at the venue, surpassing England’s 112 there last year.Pakistan’s reply was built around an 80-run opening partnership between Tayyab Arif and Azan Awais.Tayyab made 46 before the visitors struck back in the final session, removing three wickets. Awais remained unbeaten on 47 at stumps, alongside nightwatchman Saqib Khan, who was on two.The day had begun with Sri Lanka struggling to cope with Pakistan’s pace and movement.Saqib, who took seven wickets on debut in the drawn first Test, made the early breakthrough in the fourth over, drawing an edge from Pasindu Sooriyabandara, who made two, for wicketkeeper Ghazi Ghori to take the catch.Abbas then removed the experienced Dinesh Chandimal, caught at short leg by Awais for seven, before Kamindu Mendis edged to Tayyab at short cover for eight. Sri Lanka were 25-3 and under mounting pressure.Razaullah made further inroads to leave the visitors reeling at 36-5. Opener Lahiru Udara, who had laboured for 34 balls to make four, was caught by Mohammad Taha at first slip, while first-Test centurion Dhananjaya de Silva was trapped leg-before for one.Kusal Mendis and Sonal Dinusha offered the only meaningful resistance, adding 49 for the sixth wicket to give the innings some substance.Kusal top-scored with 32 from 50 balls, hitting five fours, while Dinusha made 21 from 40 deliveries with four boundaries.The partnership was ended by Jamal, who dismissed Kusal with a short delivery that produced a miscued hook.Dinusha fell to the same bowler in similar fashion, pulling a short ball to a fielder in the deep. Their departures triggered another collapse, with Sri Lanka losing their last four wickets for just 13 runs.Razaullah bowled Milan Rathnayake without scoring, Abbas took a return catch to dismiss Prabath Jayasuriya for three, and Jamal completed the innings by removing Lahiru Kumara.Abbas finished with 3-14, Razaullah took 3-21 and Jamal returned 3-24, while Saqib claimed the other wicket.Pakistan’s openers initially had to negotiate movement from the new ball, with Rathnayake particularly disciplined in keeping them quiet.But Tayyab and Awais settled in and gradually found their scoring rhythm, putting together an 80-run stand that gave the hosts a strong start in pursuit of Sri Lanka’s modest total.Tayyab was the more fluent of the two, finding boundaries with confident strokeplay, while Awais also began to open up as the innings progressed.Their partnership put Pakistan in a commanding position before Sri Lanka found a way back in the final session.Spinner Prabath Jayasuriya broke the stand by dismissing Taha for eight. Captain Babar Azam then fell for the same score, bowled by Lahiru Kumara after leaving a delivery that went on to hit the stumps.Awais, however, remained at the crease to guide Pakistan beyond Sri Lanka’s total. With the hosts on 121-3 when bad light brought play to an end, he was unbeaten on 47, while Saqib had joined him at the other end.Sri Lanka bowling coach Ryan van Niekerk described the first-innings collapse as a shock, saying his side had not expected to be dismissed for fewer than 100 in a Test.He said the priority was to fight back with attacking bowling and take early wickets on the second morning, adding that claiming four wickets in a session would be a positive response.Jamal praised the surface for offering assistance to the fast bowlers and said Pakistan had made the most of winning the toss. He remained confident that the hosts could build a substantial lead despite losing three wickets.The first Test of the two-match series ended in a draw. Tuesday also brought a setback for both teams in the World Test Championship, as they were fined and docked points for slow over-rates.Sri Lanka lost 15 points, slipping from seventh to eighth in the nine-team standings, while Pakistan were deducted five points after falling five overs short. They remained ninth and last.

headline: CDF Munir underscores importance of sustained engagement, mutual trust in meeting with Iran’s Araghchi
summary: Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir underscored the importance of sustained engagement, mutual trust and close coordination between the two countries to promote regional peace and stability during a meeting with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, the military’s media wing said on Tuesday.According to astatementissued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), matters of mutual interest, regional security dynamics and evolving geopolitical developments were also discussed between the two.Both sides also exchanged views on exploring avenues to address common security challenges, it added.Araghchi appreciated Pakistan’s “constructive role in promoting regional peace and stability and expressed his country’s desire to further strengthen bilateral relations”, ISPR said.Pakistan has been mediating between Washington and Tehran, making efforts for an end to a war that began with US attacks on Iran on February 28.Months of diplomacy have failed to resolve the war, while CDF Munir has been playing a key role in Pakistan’s mediation efforts.His latest meeting with Araghchi took place in Rawalpindi on Monday, when the Iranian foreign minister was in Pakistan, primarily to attend the 30th meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) Council of Foreign Ministers.During his visit, the Iranian foreign ministerexpressedconfidence in Pakistan’s role in the mediation and said Tehran trusted Islamabad as a “good friend”.Islamabad is doing its job and Iran is satisfied with its engagement, he said.Prior to Monday’s meeting, CDF Munir’s most significant engagement with the Iranians took place last month inTehran. He was in the Iranian capital along with other officials from member countries of the Makkah defence pact — a tripartite agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye.The discussions had taken place against a backdrop of heightened concern over the escalating conflict between Yemen’s Ansar Allah rebels and Saudi Arabia, the security of the Strait of Hormuz and the prospect of renewed US and Israeli military action against Iran.It was decided during the meeting that all participating sides would “continue their dialogue to bolster cooperation among the four regional nations, including in the areas of regional peace and security.”Officials from Pakistan, including the CDF, have undertaken multiple visits to Iran after the war began. The defence forces chiefvisitedIran on Oct 21 as well. During that visit, Iranian leaders conveyed to him that the US must take the first steps to rebuild trust and that the acceptance by Washington of Tehran’s seven-point proposal for working towards peace could provide a starting point for renewed negotiations.He earliertravelledto Tehran on Aug 24 and met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Araghchi and other senior officials to discuss regional security and efforts to restore stability.Pakistan’s mediationPakistan’s efforts for peace between the two sides began soon after the war.Less than two months after the war started, Pakistan brokered a ceasefire between the two sides on April 8 andIslamabad hosted direct talksbetween US and Iran on April 11 and 12.The mediation efforts also led to the signing of theIslamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)on June 17 between the US and Iran in Geneva.The MoU set a framework to move towards a permanent end to the war.While hostilities later renewed between the two sides, Pakistan remained engaged in mediation efforts.Currently, however, a stalemate remains in the negotiations between the US and Iran.But Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Monday that Islamabad had not given up on its diplomatic efforts for a peaceful resolution to the US-Iran war.Dar said he had “very candid, very frank, very brotherly, very comprehensive discussions” with Araghchi on the sidelines of the ECO meeting.Noting that the two discussed the latest regional situation, the deputy premier said Iran had “fast-tracked” itsseven-day proposalto reopen the Strait of Hormuz to atwo-day plan.“So, the response from the United States is pending. We have not given up hope or efforts. We are still doing our best [so] that the situation gets sorted out,” DPM Dar stated.He also expressed hope that, now that Washington was no longer busy with its midterm elections, it would respond to the proposal “very soon”.

headline: Shane Deitz appointed Pakistan women’s team head coach
summary: The Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) on Tuesday appointed Australian Shane Deitz as head coach of the national women’s cricket team, with the 51-year-old set to take charge ahead of the forthcoming bilateral series against West Indies.Deitz will join the Pakistan squad in the Caribbean for his first assignment, replacing Wahab Riaz, who had been serving as mentor and head coach following the departure of former Test batter Mohammad Wasim after last year’s ICC Women’s World Cup.He becomes the third foreign coach to take charge of the Pakistan women’s team, following New Zealand’s Mark Coles, who had two stints in the role, and Bermuda’s David Hemp. His appointment also marks a return to a foreign coaching option after a period of local coaches.In a statement issued by the PCB, Deitz said he was honoured to take up the position, recalling his memories of supporting Pakistan during the 1992 World Cup final against England.“I am very honoured to become the head coach of the Pakistan women’s team. Pakistan cricket has a tremendous history and I remember fondly cheering them on as a youngster in Australia at the 1992 World Cup final against England, which was a great achievement for Pakistan cricket,” he said.Deitz said the team’s long-term objective would be to give supporters something to cheer about when Pakistan hosts the T20 World Cup in 2028. He acknowledged that considerable work lay ahead for the players and coaching staff to produce world-class performances.Playing and coaching backgroundHailing from Bankstown, New South Wales, Deitz was a left-handed top-order batter who also occasionally kept wickets.After representing New South Wales at junior level, he moved to South Australia, where he played 66 first-class matches for the Redbacks between 1998-99 and 2007-08.Following his retirement, Deitz moved into coaching, initially serving as a high-performance coach with Cricket Wellington in New Zealand from 2008 to 2013.He subsequently coached Bangladesh’s women’s team in 2013-14 before taking up various roles with Vanuatu Cricket, including national coach and chief executive.From around 2020 to 2023, he coached the Netherlands women’s team, helping the side regain ODI status.In July 2023, Deitz was appointed head coach of the West Indies women’s team. Under his guidance, the Caribbean side reached the semi-finals of consecutive ICC Women’s T20 World Cups in 2024 and 2026.His contract with Cricket West Indies expired at the end of October 2026, with both parties mutually agreeing to part ways.Frequent changes in coaching set-upThe Pakistan women’s team has witnessed considerable instability in its coaching set-up in recent years, with Deitz becoming the sixth person to take charge in the past three and a half years.Coles, the first foreign coach of the team, served from 2017 to 2019 before briefly returning in 2023. However, he resigned during his second stint for personal reasons.Hemp succeeded Coles and remained in the role from 2020 until around 2022.Subsequent appointments included local coaches and interim arrangements, with Wasim taking charge ahead of the 2024 Asia Cup before his departure following the World Cup.Wahab subsequently oversaw the team as mentor and head coach during a mixed period that included a solitary victory at the T20 World Cup, a semi-final appearance at the Asia Cup and a bronze medal at the Asian Games, alongside a number of series defeats.Pakistan are currently featuring in the ICC Emerging Nations Trophy in the United Arab Emirates.

headline: French cricket 'dying' as federation crisis and chaos deepens
summary: Cricket in France is at risk of disappearing altogether, less than two years before the sport makes its long-awaited Olympic return.The last, and only time that cricket was played at the Olympics was in Paris in 1900, where England beat France by 158 runs to win the gold medal.France will not be at the Twenty20 tournament at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, and cricket in the country is on the verge of “dying” due to a crisis within the country’s federation, Miriam Romero, a player and administrator, toldAFP.Clubs suspended the national league this year as they try to force president Prebagarane ‘Prebou’ Balane to resign following a series of scandals.The organisation lost its recognition by France’s sports ministry early this year, while the International Cricket Council (ICC) in June suspended development funding and placed France Cricket on notice for “non-compliance with membership criteria”.This came after scandals such as ‘ghost’ women’s matches and development funding that was unaccounted for.“We must not let cricket die in France, it’s a shame,” Romero, who is president of the Paris regional cricket committee, toldAFP.“If we don’t do anything (it will die).”Romero, who at 65 still plays, was previously on France Cricket’s finance committee and is also a director at Paris Universitaire Club (PUC), one of the main cricket clubs in France.She says PUC and other clubs have left France Cricket and are trying to set up a new national association to replace the existing structure.Others, though, simply want Balane to resign so they can resolve the governance issues that saw them lose recognition from the ICC and the sports ministry.According to the minutes of a board meeting in June, seen by theFrance 24television station before it was deleted from the France Cricket website, Balane said he would resign on July 17.But board member Jubaid Ahamed said Balane had not fulfilled his promise.Despite repeated attempts byAFPto contact Balane and France Cricket, neither replied.The chaos led the main clubs in France Cricket’s domestic championship to suspend the competition in mid-August, meaning the season was never completed.They have had enough and their demands are simple: “Firstly, to change the president. Then, to restructure France Cricket by implementing more flexible rules to develop youth and women’s cricket,” Djega Sankaran, the former president of the Morangis club, south of Paris, said.He said he had resigned so he could speak freely without repercussions for his club.AFPspoke to the president of the France Gymkhana club, Rizwan Babri, the president of another club and the team manager from a third club who all confirmed they wanted Balane to resign and for France Cricket to be restructured.One person described Balane as acting like “God Almighty”, another accused him of treating the federation as “his private affair”.In November, 34 clubs — more than enough to reach the necessary one third threshold — asked France Cricket for an extraordinary general meeting to submit a motion of no confidence in Balane and the executive committee, but the president refused, in email responses seen byAFP.‘Cry babies’The crisis had been brewing for some time.It began whenFrance 24broke an explosive story in 2023 about clubs in the country faking women’s matches, apparently so France Cricket could benefit from hundreds of thousands of dollars of ICC funding.The national women’s cricket team wrote an open letter demanding an investigation and accountability, but instead, France Cricket suspended them.“What was sad for us was that the men, the other clubs, did not support us,” Sabine Lieury, a former French women’s international and ex-president of Nantes Cricket Club, toldAFP.“The cricket world didn’t want to rebel with the French girls to say that this was unacceptable.”Worst of all, the men’s national team accused the women of being “cry babies” and disloyal.“No one did anything, they kept playing to protect themselves.”But they changed their tune after France Cricket lost its ICC development funding and French government recognition.France Cricket have always denied that women’s ghost matches took place — Balane told theBBCin June that it had “never” happened.But that was not true. In fact, it was still happening last year.The problem was that the federation obliged clubs to set up a women’s team and threatened them with fines or even demotion if they did not fulfil fixtures.Some clubs tried, but there was not the necessary interest to do so in such a tight timeframe.“Everyone brought women’s teams one way or another, with cousins, but it was just to avoid Prebou’s sanctions,” said Sankaran, who was heavily involved in trying to develop cricket in the Ile de France region around Paris.“There were six people here, four people there. There were no (real) matches.”In the end, it was easier not to have a women’s team.“There were agreements between clubs: ‘You won’t get a fine and I won’t get a fine’. They made up the scores,” said Sankaran.“All the clubs made mistakes, me included.”‘Not surprised’But those who were playing had always been suspicious.There were four teams in the French women’s first division at that time: Nantes, PUC, Lille and Lisses. But there were nine teams in the second division, and none were ever promoted.“How is it that every year, we never see someone coming from these second division teams?” said Lieury.“When the scandal broke, we were shocked, but at the same time, we said: ‘we’re not surprised, we’ve never seen these girls’.”Even in 2024 and 2025, only two clubs — PUC and AC Stains — could muster a full women’s team and genuinely fulfil fixtures.Tara Britton, a former Lisses and France player who subsequently joined PUC, said the only genuine match her new team played was against Stains.The other teams either did not turn up, did so without enough players, or wanted to play with a tennis ball rather than a cricket ball.The France Cricket website lists the results from 2024 and 2025 with PUC as the champions and Stains as the beaten “finalists”.But Britton said those seasons essentially amounted to a single match.And then there is the question of the ICC development funding.Numerous clubs toldAFPthat they never received any help from France Cricket. Sankaran said the organisation even refused to contribute to the purchase of a plastic wicket or cricket nets, offering only a loan instead.

headline: Trump is not going to let Iran conflict become a 'forever war', asserts Vance
summary: US Vice President JD Vance said on Monday that President Donald Trump will not allow the ongoing war on Iran to turn into a prolonged military commitment, rejecting calls for an extended US presence and insisting that the administration remains committed to avoiding another “forever war”.In an interview withFox News, Vance said there was no disagreement between him and Trump over the direction of the conflict, emphasising that the president intends to bring the war to an end rather than allow it to become a long-term engagement.“My prediction is that whatever the president ultimately decides to do, there are going to be people who demand more, who want the war to go on indefinitely,” he said.“What I feel quite confident about the president of the United States — and again, there’s no daylight here — is that whatever he ultimately decides to do, however he ultimately decides to bring the conflict to a close, he is not going to let this become a forever war,” he added.Vance’s comments come as the US and Iran remain locked in a conflict while debate intensifies over it costs and duration.“We are not going to allow this to become a 10- or 15-year commitment, or frankly, even a two-year commitment,” Vance said.He accused some critics and foreign policy advocates of wanting the US to remain engaged indefinitely, adding that the administration had made a clear commitment to voters to avoid prolonged overseas wars.“Despite the fact that a lot of neoconservatives and a lot of other people want us to stay there forever, we’re not going to stay there forever. We promised we wouldn’t,” he said.Vance also expressed confidence that Trump would ultimately end the war with “great results” for the American people.‘I’m happy to be a heat shield’ for TrumpDuring the interview, Vance also addressed criticism surrounding the administration’s handling of the Iran conflict and its potential political consequences for Republicans following the2026 midterm elections.Asked whether there were differences between him and Trump over the war, he rejected the suggestion, saying there was no disagreement among senior administration officials.He acknowledged, however, that the conflict had carried political costs, particularly through higher gasoline and energy prices.“Politically, yes, and I think the president himself has absolutely said this as well. There was a political cost: the higher gas prices, the higher energy prices,” he said.The vice president also pushed back against criticism directed at him over a memorandum of understanding related to Iran, suggesting that some critics were using him as a substitute target for attacking Trump.“I’m happy to be a heat shield for the president of the United States,” Vance said.

headline: West Bank’s displaced Palestinians hold little hope for post-Netanyahu era
summary: After Israeli forces pushed him and thousands of others out of the West Bank refugee camp of Tulkarem last year, Adel Darsieh held onto his hope of returning home, but it is fading fast.Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed no return for the displaced people from the camp near the northern city of Jenin, claimed to be a hub for Palestinian fighters.He is now fighting for his political life after his party lost seats in Israel’s general election last month and former generalGadi Eisenkotwas tasked with trying to form a new government.But even the prospect of an end to Netanyahu’s rule is not enough to lift Darsieh’s hopes.“Whether it’s this government or a new one, what does it change?” said the 64-year-old.“They’re two sides of the same coin.”The Israeli military carried out a major operation in the north of theoccupied Palestinian territoryin early 2025, during atemporary ceasefirein Gaza, having vowed to root out alleged fighters.Shortly before the election, Netanyahu announced that no one removed from Tulkarem would be allowed back.Displaced Palestinians from Tulkarem refugee camp wait outside a charitable association to receive food, near the city of Tulkarem in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, on November 11, 2026. —AFPFor Palestinian families, it is a second form of displacement. The Tulkarem camp was set up in 1950 for refugees who fled or were forced out during the creation of the state of Israel two years earlier. The West Bank has been occupied by Israel since 1967.“Successive generations have lived through displacement without being able to return to their homes. If our grandparents and parents couldn’t return, how can we believe that our return will be possible?” Darsieh said.According to UN figures, the Israeli operation launched last year displaced 12,100 people from the Tulkarem camp.‘Empty stomachs’With the Israeli military keeping up periodic operations around the region, Darsieh is living near the camp in a modest, makeshift home with a sheet metal roof. His wife uses a wheelchair.He went to receive trays of mansaf, a dish of rice, meat and fermented yoghurt, prepared by Fazaa Kitchen, a solidarity group that serves food to the displaced.Working from the building of the Wadi al-Hawarith charity, volunteers in orange jackets fill, seal and package portions of food in an assembly line.The group prepares and distributes some 1,200 meals to 400 families.“If we weren’t cooking, families would be going to bed with empty stomachs,” said the organisation’s head, Hussein al-Sheikh Ali, 60, who himself is displaced.Members of a charity project prepare meals for internally displaced Palestinians from Tulkarem refugee camp, near the city of Tulkarem in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, on November 11, 2026. —AFPHe described Israel’s actions in the West Bank since the Gaza war  as “collective punishment”.Netanyahu’s caretaker government, which includes far-right figures, rapidly expanded Israeli settlements in the West Bank which are considered illegal under international law.“Some Palestinians hope that a new Israeli government might emerge with a less extremist, more moderate tone,” Ali said.“Yet the fear remains that the same policies towards the Palestinians will persist, even if the political figures themselves change.”A child stands in the remains of the house of a Palestinian who was accused of possessing a rocket, according to his family, after it was demolished by Israeli forces, in Kafr Nima, near Ramallah, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on November 16, 2026. —ReutersFaisal Salama, who heads Tulkarem camp’s popular committee, which represents residents, called Netanyahu’s decision to stop residents returning illegal.But he held out guarded hope for an end to military operations. He pointed to how Israel, soon after the election, ended an operation in Hebron that displaced 3,000 Palestinians, which was launched after gunmen shot dead two Israeli soldiers.‘Scale of suffering’Even if residents could return, much of the camp has been destroyed. Houses have been razed, buildings emptied and businesses burnt down.Eisenkot, who commanded forces in the West Bank during the secondIntifada, a Palestinian uprising from 2000 to 2005, has sought to appeal to a broad spectrum, including liberals, but has only taken some distance from Netanyahu on security.Eisenkot backs the existence of the major settlements but has also spoken out forcefully against extremist settlers who have attacked Palestinians with virtual impunity.Flames appear during an explosion as Israeli forces demolish the house of a Palestinian who was accused of possessing a rocket, according to his family, in Kafr Nima, near Ramallah, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on November 16, 2026. —ReutersBeth Oppenheim, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said a consensus has emerged among Jewish Israelis on key policies on the West Bank, including opposition to the creation of a Palestinian state.Still, she said that Eisenkot as prime minister could be more flexible on allowing a return to Tulkarem.“I think that given the political atmosphere in Israel today, this will be done through a security pretext,” she said.“They would make the case that this is necessary to stabilise the situation in the West Bank and that having people displaced could create the conditions for unrest,” she said.For Asia Assaf, 44, a Fazaa Kitchen volunteer whose home was destroyed in March 2025, political debates are far away from her daily concerns.“One cannot truly grasp the scale of suffering until one has experienced it firsthand,” she said.

headline: Gamers in Asia stoked to play 'GTA VI', many on grey market
summary: It’s censored in Japan, not officially sold in China, and has floundered in Asian markets where mobile games are king, but “Grand Theft Auto” fever is sweeping the continent regardless.Excitement among gamers in Asia for Thursday’s “GTA VI” mega-release shows how the industry has evolved since the fifth installment in 2013, and quashes the idea that cultural aversion to lawless escapades holds it back, analysts say.“The game was part of my youth,” Yang Hauiyu, a market research professional in Beijing, toldAFP, recalling playing a pirated PC version non-stop as a teen.A shopkeeper in New Delhi prepares for the launch of ’Grand Theft Auto VI. —AFPLike others worldwide, Yang, now in his 30s, pre-downloaded “GTA VI” for his PlayStation – even though the video game is not licensed for sale in mainland China.PlayingGTAis not banned, but as with most Western-made games, the series, notorious for its violent scenarios, has never obtained government approval.However, a large grey market forGTAexists in the world’s second-largest economy.Fans access it via servers in Hong Kong and elsewhere while authorities turn a blind eye, even as the series’ popularity balloons, said Shenzhen-based gaming consultant Daniel Camilo.“The console market was minuscule in China and now it’s much bigger,” he said, adding that the middle class has grown since 2013 and younger gamers are more open to global pop culture.Advertising for the video game “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) is seen in Seoul on November 10, 2026. —AFPCamilo predicted “GTA VI” could be the firstGTAgame with a significant commercial impact from China — the country with the globe’s highest gaming revenues, according to industry analysis firm Newzoo.He estimated sales of two to five million copies from the nation, a figure which is “virtually impossible to track”.Z-ratedIn Thailand, whereGTAsales were suspended in 2008 after an alleged copycat murder of a taxi driver, one Bangkok gaming centre is now advertising “GTA VI” sessions from launch day.But for some, the heavily American themes in the US-published series are off-putting.Donghwi Kim, a 23-year-old South Korean student, is a big fan of Nintendo’s “Zelda” games, but has not triedGTA.“It’s focused on the United States’ culture, right?” he said. “I don’t have interest in that”.In Japan, home of the PlayStation, “GTA V” was the seventh top-selling game in the 2013-14 financial year, below six Japanese-made rivals, gaming magazine Famitsu reported.Commuters walk past advertising for the game “Grand Theft Auto VI” by US studio Rockstar Games at a train station in Singapore on November 17, 2026. —AFPIn contrast,“GTA V” was the “best-selling console video game of 2013 in North America, Latin America and Europe combined”, its publisher said at the time.The game is censored on consoles in Japan to comply with strict explicit-content rules that refuse to classify works depicting genitals, sexual acts or prostitution in a positive light.To obtain a “Z-rated” — adult-only — classification, Japan’s “GTA V” replaces a sexual act with smoking a cigarette, shows strippers with their breasts covered, and cuts torture scenes short.Although nothing is yet confirmed, censorship rumours were fuelled for “GTA VI” because the Japanese version is around a gigabyte smaller than the international one.‘Enormous’ anticipationFor Indian players used to navigating chaotic traffic, overloaded motorbikes and daredevil overtaking, the game’s high-speed chases hold a particular appeal.India’s gaming market generated $2.7 billion in 2024, and more than half a billion people played in the past year, according to separate government and industry figures.But more than 90 per cent of Indian gamers use mobile phones — making the console-owning audience for a blockbuster such as “GTA VI” a much smaller, more affluent group.A red Chevrolet Camaro drives past a “Vice City” sign in the Wynwood neighborhood, ahead of the release of the video game Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI), in Miami, Florida, US, November 16, 2026. —AFPIndian fans are celebrating the launch with gaming marathons and unofficial parties, including a Vice City-inspired night in tech hub Chennai featuring virtual-reality gaming, superbikes and live graffiti.“The anticipation is enormous,” said party organiser Fahad Saud, 35, who grew up playing GTA’s multiple editions.“In India, where the day-to-day struggle is so great,GTAgives us the avenue to vent the pressure, to have space and freedom.”PC vs console“GTAhas historically had a smaller share of the overall gaming market in many Asian countries compared to North America and Europe,” said Daniel Ahmad, director of research and insights at Niko Partners.But its popularity “is driven more by differences in gaming platforms, business models, and spending habits than cultural preferences”, he toldAFP.This illustration picture taken on November 15, 2026 in Bangkok shows the home menu of the PlayStation 5 (PS5) with a countdown (bottom L) for the video game “Grand Theft Auto (GTA) VI”The high cost is a barrier, and at launch “GTA VI” is only coming to consoles — a gadget that plays a smaller role in many Asian markets.“We expect the launch to generate significantly greater attention in Asia than previous entries in the franchise,” Ahmad said.However, “much of the fanfare will be reserved for the PC launch, given the larger PC gaming audience”.Indonesian Jonathan Nainggolan, 34, asked his wife’s permission to purchase the game’s “ultimate edition”, which costs around $80 in the country.“I expect to play the game continuously… probably, until the end of the year, I will try to completeGTA VI.”
